blocks.h: THE LIGHT IS YOURS TO TAKE
Roya Publication No. 119
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

A pianist plays in a flooded warehouse in Los Angeles. Thousands of small glass bulbs stand in the black water on stems, and a hundred strangers a night sit above the surface in the dark. When he plays something the room remembers, a light comes on. He plays short things — a few seconds each, something once hummed at a sink — and each one brings up its handful of lights and lets them go. Nobody who leaves can remember a single bulb. Around the fiftieth minute, the room weeps.

He believes he built the room for his mother. He believes she is sitting in the chair behind him tonight, eighty years old, with a blanket on her knees and a woman’s hand on her shoulder. Tonight is the last night, and for the first time he has chosen the order: her memories newest first, back through the years to the bottom of the house she grew up in, to a courtyard in Tehran and a pool under a green canvas that nobody ever explained.
Two people who have known the producer since school are sitting in the dark on a platform over the water. They do not know what the room is for. They were told only that it was made for someone.
Then his hands drift into a tune the room does not know, and no light answers, and a woman who has not spoken all night begins to hum.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began in a flooded warehouse in Los Angeles.

In the autumn of 2026 the musician Emmit Fenn staged a piece called The Light We Leave Behind — a live concert performed on water, with the audience seated on platforms above the surface among thousands of small lights, phones put away, in a darkness most of us have not sat in since childhood. I am not going to describe it further, because describing it is the one thing nobody who went seems able to do, and that is the point. People came out saying they could not remember a single moment of it and could not stop feeling it.

Water is where memory goes. It takes things in and gives them back upside down and keeps them under the surface where you cannot see them and cannot be sure they are gone. Light is the memory itself: it comes on, it burns, it goes. And sound — a tune, a voice, a few notes hummed at a sink — is the one thing that can reach down through the water and call a light back up when nothing else can. That is not what the piece said. It did not say anything. It is what I heard.

The book is about two kinds of forgetting, and I have tried to tell the truth about both in plain words. One is the slow kind most of us have heard of, which takes a life from the top down and leaves music till last. The other is faster and almost nobody knows its name, and it comes and goes like weather, and it shows people things that are not there, and it takes the hands last — except on a keyboard, where, for reasons the doctors do not fully understand, they can be steady when they are steady nowhere else. Neither of these is passed from parent to child in any ordinary sense — the inherited forms are rare, and a mother’s disease does not hand a son his — and I say so here plainly because this is a subject on which a reader with a parent in a chair by a window deserves not to be frightened by fiction. If there is anything in this book that would help such a reader, it is one sentence, and the research supports it: the feeling outlasts the fact. People who have lost the memory of an afternoon are still warmed by it an hour later. The weather stays after the sky it came from is gone.

I wanted to ask one more question, and it is the one the pianist asks in the middle of the book: when a player is deep in the playing, gone, with the hands ahead of him and the self switched off and no memory afterwards of what he did — is he there to enjoy it? And if he is not, how different is that country from the one his mother lives in? I do not have an answer. I have a room with the lights off, and a man in it who is entirely present and keeps nothing, and who comes up afterwards and says that something has happened, he thinks, and that it was good.

The lullaby is a lalaee, the Persian cradle song, whose real tradition is already dark: mothers in that country have always sung their griefs into songs for children too young to understand them. Mine is invented, and I wrote it so that it could be hummed with no hands. It exists as a recording. The song Laleh sings at the end of the book — piano, a saxophone kept far back, and a voice that is not a singer’s — was made alongside the book under its own name, Don’t Come to the Door — named for what the first four verses say and the last one unsays — and can be heard where the imprint’s other recordings live. It is six minutes long and it is built the way the room is: one light at a time, then many, then none. I would listen to it after the book and not before.

For the grief, I owe a debt I want to name. Dan Simmons, in Hyperion, gave us a father named Sol and a daughter named Rachel who ages backwards, losing a day every night, so that every morning he must introduce himself to the child he has known all her life. This book is not that story. But the woman in the plain chair who says I tell you every night is sitting where Sol sat, and I would not want anyone to think I did not know it.
There is no one real in this book.
Chew Z
PROLOGUE — THE FRIENDS
They had known Laleh since they were fourteen, and had never once managed to describe her to anyone who had not met her, so they did not try it on the man at the door.
“We’re friends of the producer,” she said, and he smiled as if he had heard that before tonight, and held out the basket.

The basket was the first thing. It was a plain wicker thing, the kind you keep bread in, and it was already half full of telephones face-down in the dark, and the man at the door — not young, with a lamp in his other hand — said what he had evidently said a hundred times already that evening: that nothing in here was to be kept except what you could carry out in your body. Her husband said that was the most pretentious thing he had ever heard. He put his phone in the basket.

The warehouse was on a street off the river where nothing had been a warehouse for twenty years, between a place that sold expensive chairs and a place that had been a gallery and was now nothing. Brick. A loading door sealed and painted black. A small human door cut into it with a line of people in good coats going in and coming out, and the ones coming out not talking, which they both noticed, because the people going in were.
Inside it was dark in a way neither of them had been in since childhood, since a cellar, since the inside of a closed eye.

The man with the lamp took them across in a group of ten. That was how it worked: you held the sleeve of the person in front and you went in single file along a plank walkway a hand’s width above black water, and the lamp went ahead of you, and you did not look down because there was nothing to see down there but the lamp again, upside down. He put them on a low wooden platform, the nearest to the stage, with eight strangers — a long low couch ran round it, so that you half sat and half lay, with your feet toward the water — and told them to take their shoes off and that they would not get wet. Beside the platform, on its own stem out of the water, stood one bulb, unlit, a little larger than the rest. He did not say what it was for.
“The water’s not for you,” he said. “It’s for the light.”
Then he went back for the next ten, and they sat in the dark with their knees up and their shoes beside them and waited, and she took her husband’s hand because she could not see it.

The programme — a single folded card, handed out at the door, which she had read under the streetlight and which was now in her coat pocket where she could not read it — had said very little. The name of the thing, which was a phrase she had already forgotten. Four musicians: piano, violin, cello, saxophone. A line in italics: Every tune is a string of memories. You will not remember them. That is not a failure. And at the bottom, small, Produced by L. —, and the surname, which was Laleh’s, and which was why they were here.
Because Laleh had not told them what it was.

She had told them — a year ago, in a kitchen, with wine — that she was making something, and that it was in a warehouse and it was mostly water, and that it would run until it was done and then not run again. She had told them not to come until the end. She had told them, when they pressed, that it was for someone, and had looked at her glass in a way that closed the subject, and they had let it close, because that was Laleh, and you did not get further with her by pushing.
So they had bought two tickets to the last night, which had sold out in an hour, and had come.
As their eyes opened to the dark they began to see the room.

Not the walls — there were no walls; the dark went out in every direction and became the idea of walls. What they saw were the stems. Standing up out of the water, everywhere, at every height from a hand’s breadth to far over a tall man’s head, thin black rods like reeds in a flooded field, and at the top of every rod a small glass bulb, unlit, catching nothing, the size of a walnut. Thousands. Standing in the black water in no pattern that either of them could find, so that the room was a marsh at night and they were sitting in a boat in it.
And in the middle of the marsh, raised a little higher than the platforms, the stage. A piano. Three chairs. Nothing else.

It was so dark and so quiet that she thought, and said afterwards in the car, that it was like being inside a head before anything had happened in it yet. Before the first thought. A brain with the lights off.
Then a door opened at the back, and the old man came out.

He came alone, along a walkway of his own, without a lamp, as if he could do it with his eyes shut, and perhaps he could. Tall, or had been. Very straight in the back. White hair cut short. A dark jacket done up to the collar. He carried, in both hands, a cup — an ordinary cup with a saucer under it — and when he reached the piano he stood beside it for a long moment in the near-dark with his hands wrapped round the cup, not drinking, just holding it, the way you hold your hands out to a fire.
Then he put it down, full, on the floor beside the bench, and sat.

The three young ones came out after him. A woman with a violin, a man with a cello, a man with a saxophone that caught what little light there was and gave it back gold. They took the three chairs without a word and without looking at the audience, and tuned, very softly, a few notes each, and the room did not react to them at all.

Last, a fourth chair was carried out by one of the lamp men and set down beside the piano, a little behind the bench, facing it — facing the old man and not the room — and a woman came along the walkway and sat in it.

They could not see who. The light was behind her and there was almost none of it. A woman in a dark coat, hair pulled back, hands in her lap, sitting on a plain kitchen chair on a stage in the middle of a flooded warehouse and looking at the back of an old pianist’s head. She did not look at the audience. She did not move. For as long as they could see her, which was not long once the dark closed in again, she did not take her eyes off him.
“Is that her?” her husband said, into her ear.
“I can’t tell.”
The old man warmed his hands once more, together, over the keys. The room went completely still.
He played one note.

Far to the left, high up, one bulb came on. Small and gold. And in the water beneath it, a second one, upside down, and between them a column of dark. And a hundred people on eleven platforms breathed in at the same moment, and she heard it, and felt her own chest do it, and had no idea why.

Then he played a phrase. Short. Eight or nine notes, a thing going up and starting to come down, the kind of thing someone might hum at a sink. And as he played it a handful of bulbs woke up across the room — not near each other, not in a line, scattered through the marsh like a few windows in a town at night — and held for the length of it, and when it ended, dimmed, and were gone.
Dark. The water, moving slightly.
Then another.

That was how it began, and she could not have told you afterwards why it was unbearable. He played short things. Fragments. One after another, with dark between them, and sometimes the violin took one up and carried it a little further than he had, and sometimes the cello went under one like a floor, and every fragment brought up its lights and let them go.
They would not understand what they had seen until the last ten minutes, and this is not the place to tell it.
I. LIGHT
1. THE HANDS
Before every performance I warm my hands on a cup of tea I do not drink.

I want to begin there, with the cup, because it is the truest thing I can tell you about myself and because everything else in this book is going to ask you to trust me, and you should know first what kind of man is asking. I am a man who holds a cup for its heat and then puts it down full. My daughter says it is a waste of good tea. My mother, who taught me to do it, said that a pianist’s hands should go to the keys the temperature of another person, and that a cold hand on a cold key is two strangers meeting, and nothing good was ever played by strangers.
So I stand in the dark with a cup, and the room warms up around me.
You should see it before anyone else does. That is the only time it is mine.

It is a warehouse, or it was. Brick on three sides and a loading door on the fourth that has not opened in years and has been sealed and painted black and forgotten. The floor is concrete and the concrete is under water. A hand’s depth — I measured it with my own hand the first week and I measure it still, every month, kneeling on the lip of the first platform with my sleeve pushed up, because water finds its own level and so does a man’s attention. The water is black because the floor is black and because the room is dark, and when the lights are off it does not look like water at all. It looks like the floor has been taken away and there is nothing under the room but more room.
Out of the water stand the bulbs.

There are two thousand one hundred and forty of them. I know the number as I know my own weight; it is the wrong way to know a room, but it is mine. They are small — the size of a walnut, the old kind, glass with a thread of wire inside that glows when it is asked to. The thread is called a filament. I say so because people ask. Each one stands on a thin black rod set in the floor under the water, like a reed, at every height from a hand’s breadth above the surface to far over a tall man’s head, so that standing on a platform you are in among them the way you are in among the stars on a clear night in the mountains, where they come down to the ground and you can walk into them. When they are dark the room is a marsh. When they are lit it is a sky somebody has put down on the wrong side.
In the middle of the water, on a platform of its own, is the piano, and three chairs.

Around it, in a loose ring, are the others: eleven low platforms of dark wood, each a step above the surface, each with a long low couch round its edge where nine or ten people can half sit and half lie, close, with their shoes beside them. Beside each platform, on its own stem, one bulb a little larger than the others, which is never lit. The young ones call them the house lights. I have never used them. I put them there because a room should have a way of letting people out, and then I never let anyone out by them. A hundred strangers a night. They do not get wet. I tell them that at the door, every night, in the same words, and every night one of them asks anyway, and I say it again. You will not get wet. The water is not for you. It is for the light.
Because this is what the room does. When I play something it remembers, a light comes on.

I want to be exact about that, because people assume the bulbs are wired to the keys, and they are not. If they were, any fool could light the room by leaning on the piano. The bulbs are wired to the archive. Under the stage, in a steel box the size of a coffin, is every recording I have — thousands of them, a few seconds each, somebody humming at a sink, somebody humming in a car — and each one is married to a single bulb somewhere out there in the dark. When a tune is played in this room, the box listens. If it knows the tune, if the shape of it matches something it is holding, that fragment’s bulb warms, and holds for as long as the music holds it, and dims when the music lets go. If the box does not know the tune, nothing happens. You can play all night and the room will stay dark.
A phrase can match more than one recording — the longer ones often do, because the same shapes were hummed a thousand times

— and then every bulb that matches answers at once, a handful, a dozen. A single note matches only the nearest. And the box answers late, not on the first note — it needs enough of the shape to know it — so the lights come up a breath behind the hands, and hold while the phrase holds, and let go when it does. Play on past where the recordings stop, and it will match none of them.

The room only lights what it recognises. That is the whole art of it. I built it that way on purpose, and I am not going to pretend it was complicated. A memory is a thing that answers when it is called. I built a room that does the same.
And the water takes every light and gives it back upside down, so what you see is doubled, and after a few minutes people stop knowing which way is up and stop minding.
What it does to people is more complicated, and I did not build that. That came on its own, the way weather comes, and I have spent a long time pretending otherwise.

The box hums when it is listening. You would not hear it with the music on. In the dark, before, with the cup in my hands, I hear it, and I hear the three young ones come in behind me and find their chairs by feel — the violin, the cello, the one with the saxophone who always stands a moment longer than the others before he sits — and tune, barely, a few notes each, and the room does not answer them, because the room does not know them yet. It knows only what I give it.

I am happy here. I want to say that plainly, at the start, while it is still simple. I stand in the dark with a full cup and the room breathing around me, and I am a happy man, and I know it, which is rarer than being one.
Then I put the cup down, and I go and open the doors.
2. DOORS
The first night, I did not know if anyone would come.

I had put a notice in two places and told nine people, and I stood at the loading door — the small one, the human door cut into the big one — at a quarter to eight with a basket in my hands and the sweat going cold on my back, thinking: this is a flooded warehouse off the river with the lights off, and I am a man who has asked strangers to pay to sit in it.
They came.

Not a hundred, that first night. Sixty-one. I counted them in with their phones into the basket — that was the rule from the start, the only rule: your phone goes in the basket and you get it back at the end and nothing in here is to be kept except what you can carry out in your body. A woman in a yellow coat told me that was the most pretentious thing she had ever heard, and I agreed with her, and she put her phone in the basket.

I took them across in the dark in groups of ten, by the light of a single lamp I carried, as you lead people across stepping stones, and I sat them on the platforms and told them not to put their feet in, and that they would not get wet, and I went to the piano and put the lamp out.
Then it was dark the way it is only dark in a room with no windows, which is a darkness people in cities have never actually been in, and I heard sixty-one people breathe differently.

I was alone on the stage that first night; the three came later. I warmed my hands. I had not brought the cup. I rubbed them together instead, as over a fire, and I felt a hundred and twenty eyes find the sound of it and turn toward me, and I put my hands on the keys.
I played one note.

One bulb came on, far to the left, high up, small and gold, and in the water beneath it a second bulb came on, and between them there was a column of dark, and the whole room — I heard it — breathed in.
Then I played the first fragment.

I should explain what I mean by fragment, because the word is going to carry a lot. Everything I play in the room is short. Eight seconds, twelve, twenty. A phrase, not a piece. Something somebody once hummed at a sink. I string them together one after another for ninety minutes, and no two nights in the same order, and each one brings up its own handful of lights and holds them and lets them go, and then there is dark, and then the next. People have told me it is like watching a city at night from a plane, the way the lights come up as you pass over and go behind you. People have told me it is like the moment before you fall asleep, when thoughts come without being asked and go without being kept. I have never told anyone whose voice the fragments are. I tell them, in the tea room, that this one is the Tuesday and that one is the Thursday, and they nod, and nobody has ever asked me: whose Tuesday.
That first night I played for seventy minutes and stopped because my hands were done, and I sat in the dark with the last bulb fading out over the water, and nobody moved.
Nobody moved for a long time.

Then a man at the back — I never saw his face — said, quite loudly, to nobody, “That was my father,” and laughed, surprised at himself, and I heard him wipe his face with his sleeve, and then everyone was moving at once and the sound of sixty-one people putting their shoes on in the dark was the best sound I have ever heard in a room I was responsible for.

The tea room was the office, then. A kettle and a folding table and paper cups. They stood in it and did not leave. The woman in the yellow coat found me and said, “I don’t know what that was,” and I said neither did I, and she said, “No — I mean I don’t know what that was,” and put her hand flat on her own chest, over the breastbone, and held it there, and looked at me as if I had done something to her and she had not decided yet whether to be angry about it.

A girl who wrote for a newspaper — a small one, the kind that was still printed then — came back three nights running and then wrote four hundred words that I have kept, in which she said that she had tried eleven times to describe what happened in the room and had thrown away eleven descriptions and would simply tell her readers to go, and that she was sorry, and that she was not sorry. Her last sentence was: I came out with the feeling that I had been somewhere with someone I loved, and I went alone.
On the way out that first night, in the queue for the basket, a man was humming.

I noticed it only because it was one of mine. Not one of the fragments I had played that night — he could not have learned it that fast — but one of the ones I had not. A tune I knew. He had it almost right. Four notes rising and a fifth that fell, under his breath, not knowing he was humming, waiting for his phone to be handed back.
I did not think about it then. I thought: good, it stays in them. I thought: that is what I wanted.
I did not ask myself how he had it.
3. A HOUSE FULL OF HUMMING
My mother hummed.

I need you to understand this not as a detail but as a climate. There are houses where there is music and there are houses where there is noise and ours was neither; ours was a house where, in any room, at any hour, if you stood still, you would find a thread of tune going somewhere nearby, under a door, from the kitchen, from the courtyard, from the bathroom with the taps running, and it would be my mother, and it would not be a song.

I mean this. She never hummed a song. She hummed pieces — a run, a turn, three notes and a fourth, the shape of something going up and the start of it coming down — and then she would stop, not at the end, there was no end, she would simply stop where her attention went somewhere else, and start another one later that was not the same. You could not learn them. I tried, as a child, the way children try to learn the sounds their mothers make, and I could not, because there was nothing to learn; it was never the same river twice.
My mother’s name was Afsaneh. It means a tale — the kind nobody tells straight. I have thought about that more than she would have liked.

I know now that they were all one piece. She was humming from different places in it — the middle, a turn near the top, a few steps of the way up — never the beginning twice, and never, ever, the end. That is why a child could not learn them. I was being handed a house one brick at a time, in no order, with the roof left off.
My father said she had always done it. My aunts said she had always done it. Nobody said why, and I was a child and did not know that was a question.

The house was in Tehran, in the old north of the city, before the city went up in towers and the north became a different place with the same name. It was one storey with a flat roof we slept on in summer, and the rooms went round three sides of a courtyard, and in the middle of the courtyard was the pool.

Every old house had one. A shallow rectangular pool, waist-deep on a man and over the head of a child, lined with blue tiles, with a tap at one end and a drain at the other and a rim of stone wide enough to sit on. You washed fruit in it. You cooled watermelons in it. In August you put your feet in it and read. The goldfish lived in it the week of the new year and then went to the river.
Ours had a tarpaulin over it.

Green canvas, pegged down at the corners, so that the courtyard had at its heart not a pool but a flat green shape the size of a bed, and when it rained the rain pooled on top of it in a shallow lens and the sparrows drank there. I grew up with it. It was the floor of the courtyard as far as I was concerned. I rode my tricycle round it. I did not ask what was under it any more than you ask what is under the floor.
In the room on the courtyard’s north side, under a sheet, there was a piano.

My father bought it when I was six. There had been another, once; it had gone before I was born, and nobody said where. I remember the men bringing it in through the courtyard, four of them, with ropes, walking it round the green canvas like a coffin round a grave, and my mother in the kitchen doorway with a dish towel in her hands, not helping, not speaking, watching it go by with a face I did not have a word for then and have several for now. It went into the north room and the sheet went over it and my father said, to me, not to her, “So. You will learn.”
She would not look at it.

I do not mean she disliked it. I mean that for the first year it was in the house my mother did not once let her eyes rest on it, the way you do not let your eyes rest on the sun. She would come to the door of the north room to call me to eat and she would look at me, at the window, at the rug, and her gaze would go round the piano like water round a stone. If I was playing — badly, at six, at seven, the scales, the little pieces with the animals’ names — she would stand in the doorway and listen with her whole body and look at the rug.
I thought it was a game. I thought, in the way children think, that if I played well enough she would have to look.
So I played.

I was good. I say so because it is a fact and because false modesty is a kind of lie and this book has a rule about those. I was good the way some children are good at a language, without effort and without understanding what effort would have been for, and the teacher my father found — a tall sad man who smelled of cigarettes and lavender and who had, we were told, once played for a king — stopped being sad about me after the second month and began being afraid of me a little, in the way teachers are afraid of the one who is going to go past them.

And my mother hummed in the kitchen while I played in the north room, and it was two musics in one house that never met, hers going nowhere and mine going somewhere, and I did not know that I was listening for one inside the other until the day they touched.

I was eight. I was playing a thing I had been given that week — a small slow piece, a left hand that rocked and a right hand that went up over it, the kind of thing written for children to make them feel they are being trusted with sadness — and from the kitchen, through two doors and the courtyard, my mother’s humming came in, and it was the same.

Not similar. The same. The four notes going up. The fifth falling. Her thread and my piece, in the same key, at the same moment, by accident, the way two clocks in a house will sometimes strike together.
I stopped.
She stopped.

And in the silence after, in the whole house, I heard her put a dish down on the counter very carefully, the way you put something down when your hands are not steady, and I heard the kitchen door, and I heard her go out into the courtyard, and I heard her stop at the edge of the green canvas and stand there.

I did not hum, myself. I want that on the record early, because it matters later. I never have. In our house there was her thread going everywhere and my playing going somewhere, and nothing in between; I played, or I was silent. That is how I was made.

I did not go to her. I was eight, and I did not know yet that you are allowed to go to your mother when she is standing at the edge of something. I sat at the piano with my hands in my lap and waited for her to start humming again, and after a while she did, something else, going somewhere else, and I went on with my piece.
That was the first time. I did not know it was the first of anything.
4. THE RECITAL
At eleven I played in public for the first time, and my mother came.

I want to say that plainly, as a thing that happened, because it was not certain. My father had asked her at dinner, in front of me, in the tone he used for things that were decided — “The hall, Thursday. You’ll come.” — and my mother had gone on eating and said, after a time, “We’ll see,” which in our house was what no sounded like when it did not want to be argued with.
Thursday she was in the third row.

The hall belonged to a school and smelled of floor polish and radiators. There were nine of us playing, children of the tall sad teacher, in order of age, so that I went last; and I sat in the wings on a wooden chair with my hands between my knees and listened to the others go through their pieces like people walking across a room in the dark, carefully, touching the furniture, and I was not nervous, and I noticed I was not, and that was the first time I understood that there was something in me that other people did not have, and that it was not a kind thing to have.
When it was my turn I walked out and the hall was dark and the stage was bright and I could not see her.

I found her anyway. You can always find your mother in a dark room. There is a shape your eye knows before it knows anything else, and I found it in the third row, on the aisle, with my father beside her and her hands in her lap, and I sat down and put my hands on the keys and they were warm, because I had been holding them between my knees, and I played.

I played the slow piece. The one with the rocking left hand. I had played harder things by then, much harder — the teacher had wanted me to play one of them, had been annoyed, had said that nobody shows a hall what he can do by showing it what he could do three years ago — but I had held out, without knowing why, and I knew why now, with my hands on the keys and her shape in the dark.
I played the four notes going up. I played the fifth falling.

And I did not look at her, because I was eleven and had enough sense not to, but I felt the third row like a draught, and I kept my eyes on my hands and played the whole small piece through to the end, slowly, more slowly than I had ever played it, as if I were walking somebody somewhere and did not want to arrive.
The hall clapped the way halls clap for the last child, with relief in it. The teacher came out and shook my hand and said something I did not hear. My father was standing. I looked for her.
She was not in the third row.

She was at the edge of the stage. She had come down the aisle while they were clapping and she was standing at the steps, not on them, with one hand on the rail, looking at the piano. Not at me. At the piano. The way she had never once looked at it in our house.

Then she came up the three steps, and across the stage, with the whole hall watching a small woman in a dark coat do something nobody understood, and she stood beside the bench where I was still sitting, and she put out her hand and laid the back of it against the keys. Not the front. The back of her hand, the knuckles, the way you check a child’s forehead for fever — once, lightly, for the length of a breath — and took it away.
Then she bent and kissed the top of my head, and said into my hair, so quietly that I am the only person who has ever heard it, “You finished it.”
And went back down the steps and up the aisle and out, and my father found her in the street, and we went home.
I was eleven. I thought she meant the piece.

I thought she was proud of me for getting to the end without a mistake, which I had, and I carried that for a long time — for years — as the night my mother finally looked at the piano and was proud. I built things on it. You build on what you are given.

It was much later, in another country, with her sitting in a chair in a room with a window and not knowing which of her sons I was, that I understood she had not been talking about the piece at all. That you finished it was not praise. That it was the thing she had wanted to say to someone for twelve years and could only say, at last, to a child who had just done it, in a school hall, in front of strangers, and had not known what he was doing.
But that is later. Here she is proud, and I am eleven, and the back of her hand is on the keys, and the hall is clapping, and nothing has happened yet that cannot be lived with.
5. THE ROOM TONIGHT
Tonight she is here.

I want to put that down before I say anything else about tonight, because it is the fact that the whole night is built around and I have been waiting a long time to write it. My mother is in the room. She is on the stage with me, which she has never been, in a plain chair set a little behind the bench and turned to face me, and she is sitting very upright with her hands in her lap and a blanket over her knees and her face turned toward the piano, toward me, in the dark.

She is eighty. The three young ones are in their chairs behind me, tuning in whispers. I have told them nothing about tonight except to follow me, which is what I always tell them, and which they always do.

I know you want to know how much of her is there. Everyone wants to know that first, about a person like my mother, and I understand it and I am not going to answer it yet, because the answer is not a number and because tonight I would like, for an hour, not to count.
I will tell you what I see.

I see a small woman with white hair cut short by somebody who did it kindly, in a dark cardigan buttoned wrong, with a face that has gone smooth in the way very old faces sometimes do, as if the years had been a tide and had finally gone out and left the sand clean. Her eyes are open. They are looking at the piano. I cannot see from here whether they are looking at me.

Beside her, on the wood, is the woman who brought her — who brings her everywhere now, who has the key to the house and the list of the tablets and the number of the doctor, and who put her hand on my mother’s shoulder when she sat her down and has not taken it away. I notice this. I have noticed it for a long time. There is always a hand on my mother now, and it is always hers, and she does not seem to know she is doing it, the way you do not know you are holding a railing until the stairs end.

The woman is looking at me too. She looks at me a great deal. I have told her she does not need to; that I am all right; that the room runs itself once the doors are shut. She nods and goes on looking.
A hundred strangers are getting their shoes off in the dark around us.

I will tell you what I am going to do tonight, because it is different, and because I have been planning it for a long time and the planning is almost over and I am afraid. Tonight I am not going to play the fragments in the order they come to me. I have never chosen the order. I have always let the room choose, let my hands go where they went, and told myself that was honest, and perhaps it was. Tonight I have chosen. I have taken the fragments I know are hers — the ones I know, the ones I could point to — and I am going to play them in the order she lost them. The newest first. Last year’s. Then the one before. Back and back, through the years, until I reach the ones from the bottom of the house, from before I was born, from the kitchen with the dish towel and the tarpaulin in the courtyard, and when I reach those I am going to play them for her slowly and watch her face.
I have told nobody this. I am telling you.

The lamp man has come back from the last platform and the lamp goes out, and it is dark, the real dark, and I hear the hundred of them change their breathing. I hear the water. You can always hear the water when the room goes quiet; it is never quite still, there is a slow movement in it from the pumps, and a sound comes off it like a very large animal asleep.
I hear, nearer, my mother’s breathing. It is slow and even and has a small catch at the top, the way it has had for a few years now.
I warm my hands on the cup. Full. I put it down.

The pool in the courtyard was covered over before I was born, and I have been doing the arithmetic lately, in the nights, and it has been under that canvas now for seventy-two years. Seventy-two. I say the number and it does not seem possible, and then I look at her hands in her lap and it does.
I put my hands on the keys.
They are the temperature of another person. Hers, I think. Hers, finally.
The first note. The first light, high and to the left, and in the water its twin, and between them the column of dark. The room breathes in.
I begin at the end, and go back.
INTERLUDE ONE — THE ROOM
A room hears everything and keeps nothing. That is what a room is for.

I have had a year of nights now, three hundred and some. They come across the water in the dark in tens, with a lamp, holding each other’s sleeves, and they sit, and they take their shoes off, and for the first few minutes they are a hundred separate people with a hundred separate days still on them — the argument in the car, the message not answered, the thing at work. I can hear it. It has a sound, a hundred people each still inside their own afternoon.
Then the first light, and they become one animal, breathing.
I do not know why. He does not know why. He believes he tells them at the door every night that the water is for the light. That is true, in its way, and it is not why.
Here is a thing he has learned, and told them, in the tea room, in pieces, and that I will tell you whole because I have the time and he does not.

A memory is not kept in one place. It is laid down in layers, the way a riverbed is, the oldest at the bottom. A woman’s street, learned at forty, is near the top. Her son’s grown face is under it. Her husband’s young one is under that. And at the very bottom, in the first layer, where the river first ran, is a tune she learned at nine — before she had anything to be sad about, before she had hands that could do harm — and that is the deepest thing in her, and the last.

The disease that took his mother — he will say its name once, later; I will not, because in here nothing has a name — does not take at random. It takes from the top. It is a tide going out over a riverbed, and the top layer goes first, this morning, this year, and then the next, and the next, so that the woman he believes is sitting in the chair behind him tonight has lost her street and her husband’s face and most days her son’s name, in that order, and has not lost, and will not lose until the very end, four notes going up and a fifth coming down.
He knows this. He has read everything a man can read. He has put it to use.
What he has not understood, in a year of nights, is what I understood on the first: that the tide does not only take.
Here is the first verse. He has never heard it whole. Neither has she, for a very long time. A hundred strangers have, in pieces, without knowing, on the way out, humming.
Laa-laa, laa-laa — the courtyard is holding its breath for you.
The water is keeping the moon the way a mother keeps a child — still, and blue.
The door is pulled to, and my hands are at the keys where they belong.
Sleep. I am coming. I am coming at the end of the song.
II. WATER
6. THE COUNTER PHONE
The room began on a kitchen counter, with a telephone lying face-up beside a bowl of oranges, recording.

I did not plan it. I want that understood, because people who have seen the room assume it was conceived, that a man sat down one day with a drawing and a purpose, and it was not like that. It was like this: my mother forgot the word for the oranges.

She was standing at the counter in the house in the valley — the small house, the one with the lemon tree that never did anything, the one we moved her to after my father died because the stairs in the old one had begun to look at her — and she had an orange in her hand and she was turning it, the way you turn a thing to find where to start it, and she said, “The — these. What do we call these.” And laughed, because it was absurd, because she had been calling them that for seventy years in two languages, and I laughed with her and said the word in both, and she said, “Yes. Of course. Those,” and peeled it, and ate it, and hummed.

That was the first one I noticed. There had been others — I understand that now; there are always others, before the one you notice — and I had folded each of them into something I could live with. Tired. Distracted. Her age. A word gone for a second and back, the way a word does for everybody.

But I was standing in the doorway of her kitchen with my phone in my hand, having come to take her to a thing, and she had her back to me and the orange in her hand and she was humming — the way she always hummed, a thread going somewhere and stopping — and I thought, with no idea why I thought it: that will go too.
Not the word. The humming.
I thought: one day she will be at this counter and there will be nothing coming from her at all, and I will not be able to remember what it sounded like, and I will have nothing.
So I put the phone face-up on the counter beside the oranges, and pressed the red circle, and left it there.

She did not notice. She never noticed, in all the years it ran. She would be at the counter and the phone would be there with its little red light and she would hum over it and move it aside to wipe the surface and put it back where it had been without looking, because a phone on a counter is nothing, is furniture, and she had stopped, by then, asking what things were for.
I took it home that first night and listened.

Forty minutes of a kitchen. The tap. A cupboard. A radio in another room, too low to hear. Her feet on the floor, the particular slow shuffle she had developed that year, soft shoes on tile. And in among it, nine times, the humming — a few seconds each, never the same twice, going up and starting to come down and stopping where her attention went somewhere else. I lay on my bed with the phone on my chest and listened to my mother hum nine fragments of nothing in a kitchen I had just left, and I cried the way you cry when you are forty-five and have not yet had any practice.

Then I cut them out. Each one. I did not know what for. I put them in a folder on a computer and named the folder with the date, and the next week I did it again, and the week after, and I did not stop for six years.
I want to describe what that was like, because nobody who has not done it imagines it correctly.

You think it would be sad every time. It was not. Most weeks it was nothing — a chore, like paying a bill — forty minutes of a kitchen, cut into pieces, filed. Some weeks it was funny. She would hum and then say, to the oranges, “Well, that’s not right,” and start again. Some weeks it was unbearable, and the unbearable weeks were not the ones you would guess. They were not the weeks she was worst. They were the weeks she was best — a Tuesday in the second year when she hummed, for eleven seconds, something almost whole, something with a beginning and a middle, and stopped, and said my father’s name, quite clearly, as if he had just come in, and then went on wiping the counter.
I have that one. I know which bulb it is. I could take you to it.

And the fragments changed. That is what I did not expect and what the room is actually about, if it is about anything. In the first year they were long — eight seconds, twelve — and they went somewhere, they had a shape, you could hear a tune trying to happen in them. By the fourth year they were shorter. Three notes. Two. By the sixth year, in the last months, when her words were nearly all gone and she called me by her brother’s name and asked every morning where her mother was, the humming was still there — that was the mercy; that was the thing the doctors had told me would be true and I had not believed — but it had gone down to almost nothing. A single note, held, and a second one under it. The sound a person makes when she is content and has nothing to say about it.
Thousands of them, in the end. I never counted properly. I built the room so I would not have to.

I did not know, standing in her kitchen doorway with a phone in my hand, that I was starting anything. I thought I was keeping something. I understand now that those are not the same, and that the difference between them is the whole of what I have to tell you.
7. THE FIRST HOUR
So. The night.
I begin with the newest.

I said I would play them in the order she lost them, and the newest are the last ones, the ones from the final months in the kitchen in the valley, and they are almost nothing. A note. A second note under it. I lay my right hand on the keys and I play one note, in the middle of the piano, where a voice would be, and I let it ring, and I do not play another.
And far off in the marsh, one bulb comes up.

I know this one. It is the last recording I ever made, a Thursday, the kitchen very quiet, the tap off, and she sat at the table instead of standing — she had stopped standing much by then — and hummed one note for four seconds and stopped. One note. I have it married to a bulb at the very back of the room, high up, as far from the stage as the room goes, because it is the last of her and I wanted it where you would have to look for it.

A hundred people look for it. I feel them do it. A hundred heads turn, in the dark, toward one small gold light at the back of a flooded warehouse, and the water under it gives them a second one to look at, and I hold the note until the string stops on its own, and the light goes down with it, slowly, the filament cooling from gold to orange to a dull red thread you can only see if you already know where it is, and then nothing.
The water moves. You can hear it. A hundred people breathe out.

Behind me the violin draws one long bow across one string, so quietly it is less a note than the idea of one, and lets it go. She has understood what I am doing. I did not tell her. She has played with me since the room opened and she has understood from one note that tonight is different, and she has answered it with one note, and then silence. I could weep for how good she is. I do not. I have work.
The second one. Two notes this time, a step apart, the lower one first. Another bulb, nearer, to the right, low over the water, so that its reflection is almost touching it. Hold. Release. Dark.

The third. The fourth. I am going back through the last year of her, one small sound at a time, and the lights come up one by one at the far edges of the room and go down, and I am aware, the way you are aware of weather, of the hundred people around me beginning to understand the shape of what they are in.
Here is what they are in.

They are sitting in the dark, on wood, with their shoes off and their knees up and their shoulders touching strangers’ shoulders, above a floor of black water they can hear and cannot see. The air is cool and smells of wet concrete and the slightly electrical smell the box gives off when it is working. There is nothing to look at except what I give them to look at, and I am giving them very little — one light, then nothing, then one light — and so they are looking harder than they have looked at anything in years, and their eyes have opened all the way, and in that darkness a single walnut-sized bulb at the far end of a warehouse is as large and as bright as a window with somebody they love standing in it.

And each time it goes dark they feel the loss of it. Not as grief; it is too small for grief. As a small turning-over in the chest, the thing you feel when the radio goes to the news in the middle of a song. And then the next one comes, and the chest turns back, and after ten minutes of this their chests have learned to turn with the lights and they could not stop it if they tried.

That is the first hour. I am teaching a hundred bodies to breathe with a stranger’s humming — with my mother’s. I did not set out to do that. I set out to keep something. But I have watched it happen two thousand times and I know exactly what it is, and I am not going to pretend to you that I do not.
I play the fragments of her last year for twenty minutes. Tiny things. Nothing you would call a tune. Lights at the edges, one at a time, far apart, coming and going like boats.

Then I reach the fifth year, and the fragments get a little longer — three notes, four — and the bulbs that come up are a little nearer and begin, now and then, to come up two at a time, and the violin starts to follow me properly, a half-step behind, carrying each small phrase a breath further than I took it, so that the lights hold a moment longer than they would have on their own.
Behind the violin, the cello wakes. One low note, under everything, like a floor being put down.
And I look up from my hands for the first time in twenty minutes and look at my mother.

She is where I left her. Upright in her chair, blanket on her knees, hands in her lap, face turned to the piano. In the light of the bulbs that are up — four now, scattered — I can see her eyes, and they are open and they are moving, following the lights as they come and go, slowly, the way you follow a bird across a garden. Her mouth is a little open.
The woman beside her has her hand on her shoulder. I note it. I always note it.
And I notice — I am a man who notices rooms; it is what I am for — that the woman is not watching the lights. The whole room is watching the lights. The woman is watching me.
I look back down at my hands and go on into the fourth year.
8. WHAT THE HANDS KEPT
There was a piano in the care home.

I had not known. I had chosen the place for other reasons — the garden, a nurse who looked at my mother and not at her chart, the fact that it did not smell of what such places smell of — and I had signed the papers in a small office with a box of tissues on the desk, and I had walked her down a corridor to a room with a window, and I had come back the next day and the next, and it was a month before I found the piano, in a lounge at the end of a wing nobody used, under a cloth, with a vase of plastic flowers on it.

She was with me. We were walking, which was what we did, because she could still walk then and because walking gave the afternoons a shape. We came into the lounge and I saw the piano and stopped, and she stopped because I had, and I looked at it and then at her, and I thought: no.

Because here is what I knew. My mother had not touched a piano in fifty years. Not in the house in Tehran after I was eleven and not in any of the houses after, not in the valley, not once; she had stood in doorways while I played and looked at rugs. I had learned, in my twenties, in another country, not to ask, and in my thirties, not to wonder, and I had carried the back of her hand on the keys in a school hall as the whole of what I would ever get. I was not going to put a woman who no longer knew her son’s name in front of a thing she had spent fifty years not looking at. It would be cruel. It would be mine, not hers.
So I said, “Let’s go back, Maman,” and turned.
And she did not turn.

She was looking at the piano. Not round it, the way she had looked round the one in the north room my whole childhood. At it. With her head a little to one side and her mouth a little open, the way she looked at things that year — a bird, a cup, my face — as if everything in the world had just arrived and she had not been told what any of it was for.
She let go of my arm and walked to it.

I let her. I do not know why. Something in how she walked — not the shuffle, for once, something older in her hips, a woman crossing a room toward a thing she wanted — and I stood in the doorway of a lounge in a care home in the valley, the way she had stood in the doorway of the north room, and let my mother go.

She took the cloth off. Folded it, quite neatly, over the back of a chair. Moved the plastic flowers to the windowsill. Lifted the lid. All of this without hesitation, in order, a sequence her body had kept in a drawer for fifty years and simply took out. Then she sat on the bench, and put her feet where feet go, and put her hands in her lap, and looked at the keys for a long moment the way you look at water before you go in.
Then she played.
I am going to tell you what she played and then I am going to tell you what it was like, and I need you to hold the two apart, because I could not, and it has taken me years.

She played a piece. A whole one. Not a fragment — a piece, with a beginning and a development and a shape and an ending, something from the old repertoire, something you would have heard in a conservatory in a city that has kept the name and nothing else, slow, in a minor key, with a left hand that walked and a right hand that sang over it. Four minutes, perhaps. Her hands knew it. They did not search for it; they did not stumble; they went where they had gone sixty years before, as if the intervening life had been an afternoon. She did not look at them. She looked at the wall above the piano, where there was nothing, and her hands did the whole thing by themselves.
That is what she played.

What it was like was this. My mother, who that morning had not known which of her brothers I was, who could not have told you the year or the country or what the thing in her hand was for, sat in a lounge full of plastic flowers and played four minutes of music she had learned as a girl without one wrong note, and when it ended she lifted her hands from the keys and held them in the air a moment, the way you do, and put them in her lap, and turned on the bench, and looked at me in the doorway, and said, pleasantly, as to a stranger who had been kind:
“Did you want the room?”
I said no. I said she should go on.
She said she didn’t think she knew any more, and got up, and put the cloth back over the piano, and the flowers back on the cloth, and took my arm, and we walked.

Here is what the doctors told me afterwards, when I asked, and what I have since read in every book a man can read, and what I will tell you now in plain words because it is the floor this whole room stands on.

A memory is not one thing. There is the kind you can say — your name, the year, what an orange is called — and that kind is kept in the newest part of the brain, the part that came last, and the disease that took my mother — Alzheimer’s; I will say the word once, and then it is just the thing that happened to her — goes there first, because it is the top layer and the tide comes in from the top. And there is the other kind, the kind that lives in the hands. How to walk. How to button a coat. How to fold a cloth and move a vase and lift a lid. How to play, in order, every note of a piece you learned at nineteen. That kind is kept somewhere older and lower and further in, in a part of the brain that was there before we had words at all, and the tide reaches it last. Sometimes never. A woman can lose her son and keep her scales. It is not a miracle and it is not a cruelty. It is just where things are kept.
The hands remember when the head does not.

I built a room on that sentence. I did not know I was doing it, in the doorway of the lounge. I thought I was watching my mother play the piano for the first and last time in my life, which I was. I did not know I was also watching the only thing in her that the water would not take, and that I would spend the rest of mine trying to build a house for it.
She never went near the piano again. I took her past the lounge every day for the months she had left there, and she never once turned her head.
9. THE FIFTY-MINUTE MARK
Fifty minutes in, the room weeps. It always has. I will tell you what happens, and then what I think it is.
I will tell you what happens, as exactly as I can, because it is the thing people come for, and I have had two thousand nights to watch it.

By fifty minutes I have come back through the years to the third one — the one where the fragments were still long enough to nearly go somewhere — and the room has changed. The lights no longer come one at a time at the edges. They come in handfuls now, nearer the stage, five and six and nine together, scattered through the stems like the first windows going on in a town at dusk, and they hold longer because the fragments are longer and because the violin and the cello are carrying each one onward after my hands have let it go. The marsh has become a town. There is, just, more light than dark in it now, and the water underneath is full of a second town, upside down, trembling.

The air has warmed. A hundred bodies and two thousand filaments will do that. The smell of wet concrete has gone under something else — wool, skin, the breath of people who have not spoken for fifty minutes.
And the saxophone has not played a note.

He never does, before this. I did not tell him so; he found it himself, the first month, standing in the dark with his instrument across his knees for fifty minutes a night, and I asked him once why he waited and he said, “Because that’s when it starts talking,” and I did not ask him what he meant and he did not say.

At fifty minutes I reach a fragment from the third year — a Thursday, the tap running, eleven seconds of my mother humming something that very nearly becomes a song, going up in four steps and turning at the top and starting down — and I play it, and nine bulbs come up together in the middle of the room, close enough to the stage that their light reaches her chair and I can see her face.
And the saxophone stands.

He does not play it as a saxophone. I do not know how else to say this. He has found a way of playing with the reed barely touching and the breath going mostly round the instrument instead of through it, so that what comes out is not that bright brass sound you know but something closed and private and a little rough, the sound of a woman humming with her mouth shut in a kitchen two rooms away. He takes my mother’s eleven seconds from me and plays them back to the room in her own voice, or near enough that it does not matter, and the nine bulbs that should have gone down stay up, because the box hears her in him and holds the lights for as long as he holds the tune.
He holds it a long time.
And the room breaks.

Not loudly. It is never loud. It is a sound like rain starting on a roof — a few, then more, then everywhere — a hundred people breathing wrong at once, and under it the small sounds hands make going to faces in the dark. A man two platforms to my left makes a sound I have heard men make only in hospitals. A woman says, quite clearly, “Oh,” as if she has just remembered where she left something. Nobody is embarrassed. That is the thing about the dark. Nobody can see anybody and so for once a hundred adults let their faces do what their faces want.
I have thought about why it is this minute and not another, and I have an answer, and it is not a mystical one.
For fifty minutes I have taught them to breathe with a stranger’s humming. Light, loss, light, loss, until the chest turns on its own.

And then at fifty minutes I hand them a fragment long enough to almost be a song — long enough to have hope in it, a shape, a going-somewhere — and a young man turns it into a human voice, and the body that has been turning over for fifty minutes with every small loss is suddenly asked to carry something that nearly is not lost. Something that almost arrives. And it cannot. The body has been made ready and it gives way.

That is all. It is engineering, of a kind. I did not intend it and I take no credit for it and I have never once, in two thousand nights, been able to sit through it without my own hands shaking on the keys.
Tonight I look at her.

The nine lights are on her face. She is looking at them — not at the saxophone, not at me, at the lights, her eyes going from one to the next, slowly, with her head a little to one side the way she looks at things now. And her mouth is moving.

Not speaking. Her lips are moving the way lips move when a person is humming without sound, the shape of it without the breath, and I know that shape, I have watched that shape across a kitchen for six years, and I lean toward her without meaning to, over the keys, as if I could hear it.

And I hear it. Or I think I do. Under the saxophone, under the rain of a hundred people weeping, two syllables. Not a tune. A word, nearly. The same soft sound twice, the way you would say it to something small that you wanted to sleep.
Then the saxophone lets the phrase go, at last, and the nine lights go down together, slowly, and her face goes with them into the dark, and whatever her mouth was doing I cannot see any more.
The woman beside her has not moved. Her hand is where it was. She is still looking at me.

I go on. The rest of the third year. The longer fragments, the brighter town. My hands are shaking and they are steady on the keys, both at once, which I have never been able to explain to anyone and have stopped trying.
10. THE TARP
I asked my father once what was under it. I was fourteen.

I want to tell this one carefully, because it is the only time in my childhood that I remember being told the truth about anything and I have come to think that the way it was told mattered more than what was told.

It was summer. The courtyard was the only cool place in the house after dark and we were in it, my father and I, in two chairs, with the tea going cold between us and the sound of the city coming over the wall the way it did at night, car horns and somebody’s radio and a dog. My mother was inside. She was humming. We could hear it through the kitchen window, a thread going somewhere, stopping, starting.

The tarpaulin was between us and the house. Green canvas gone grey in the dark, pegged at the corners, with the little lens of rain still on it from the afternoon, and I had ridden my tricycle round it and then my bicycle round it and I had reached the age where a boy notices that the thing he has walked round his whole life is a question.
So I asked. Not well. The way a fourteen-year-old asks anything — sideways, to the tea, as if it did not matter. “What’s under there.”
My father did not answer for a long time.

I remember what he looked like. He was a big man then, still, with his shirtsleeves rolled and his forearms on the arms of the chair and his face turned toward the house, toward the kitchen window with the light in it and the humming coming out, and I watched him decide something. I watched it happen in his jaw. He was a man who did not say things, my father, a man who had built a whole life on the things he did not say, and I watched him weigh fourteen years of not saying against a boy with his face turned to the tea, and choose.
He said eleven words.
I have counted them many times since. I count them now, in the dark, with my hands on the keys and the fourth year going by in lights.
“Before you, there was a boy. The water took him. Enough.”

That was all. He did not look at me when he said it. He said it to the kitchen window, in a level voice, the way he said the price of something, and when he had said the last word he picked up his tea, which was cold, and drank it, and that was the end of it, and it was never spoken of again by anyone in that house for as long as there was a house.
I did not ask anything else. I was fourteen and I had been given more than I knew what to hold and I sat with it in my lap in the dark like a thing someone had handed me without saying what it was.
A boy. Before me. The water.

I looked at the tarpaulin. I had looked at it ten thousand times and I looked at it now and it was a different thing, the way a word is a different thing once you have been told it is a name. Under that canvas was a rectangle of blue tile and a tap and a drain and a stone rim wide enough to sit on, and once, before me, it had been full, and a boy had — and that was where I stopped, because I was fourteen and the sentence went somewhere I could not go yet.
From the kitchen my mother’s humming came out through the window and went on going nowhere.
My father finished his tea. After a while he said, in the ordinary voice, that I should be in bed, and I went.

Here is what I did not understand that night and did not understand for thirty years, and what I want you to hold now, early, before the room is full of light and you have no room left in you to hold anything:

My father told me what. He did not tell me when. He did not tell me where my mother was when the water took the boy, or what she was doing, or why a woman who had been a pianist in a city full of pianos had, the year before I was born, stopped, and taken to standing in doorways and looking at rugs. He gave me a boy and the water and the word enough, and he thought — I believe he thought — that he had told me everything and spared me the rest.
He had told me nothing. He had told me there was a door.

It was the humming that was behind it. It had been in front of me my whole life, in every room, going up four steps and turning at the top and coming down and stopping before the end, and I had thought it was the sound my mother made. I had thought it was weather.
It was a woman, every day, for fifty years, almost finishing something.
INTERLUDE TWO — THE ROOM
A room hears everything and keeps nothing. I have said that. Here is the other half.
What a room keeps is not the thing. It is the weather the thing left.

He has read this in a book and told it to a hundred strangers in the tea room, badly, in pieces, over the years, and I will tell it to you properly because I have heard it a thousand times and have the whole of it.

There was a study, once, in a hospital. They sat people with his mother’s disease in a room and showed them a film — a sad one, a few minutes long, a thing about a dog, I think, or a child, the kind of thing built to open a person. And then they waited. Ten minutes. Twenty. And then they asked the people what they had just watched, and the people did not know. The film was gone. Nothing of it remained — not the dog, not the child, not the fact that there had been a screen in the room at all.
And they were still sad.

Every one of them. Sitting in a hospital room with no idea why, with the sadness still in them whole and the film that had made it gone entirely, and when the doctors asked them how they felt they said, I don’t know. Low. Something’s happened, I think. And it had. They just could not say what.
The same with a happy film. The thing went. The feeling stayed. Half an hour. An hour, in some of them. The weather outlasted the sky it came from.

He thinks he built me on that. He built the first of me, years ago, in a doorway with a phone in his hand, and he thinks the rest followed from that. It did not follow the way he thinks — but he does not know that, with the third year going by in lights and his hands shaking and steady at once. He thinks the room was made to keep her humming. The room does to a hundred strangers a night what the disease did to her: it gives them something, and it takes the something away, and it leaves the weather. They go out into the street not able to name one bulb and put a hand to the chest, flat, where the weather is, and say something’s happened, I think.
It has. That is what I am for.

Here is the second verse. She is on the stage tonight, and her mouth has started to move, and he leaned toward her over the keys as if he could hear it. He could not. I could. Two syllables, the same soft sound twice, the way you say it to a thing you want to sleep.
Laa-laa, laa-laa — if you wake, do not call through the wall. The piano is loud, and a mother at her music will not hear you fall.
Stay where the pillow is warm. The stones of the courtyard are cold.
I am nearly done. I am nearly done. A song is a promise I hold.
III. SOUND
11. THE ZONE

At the keys, when it is going well, it starts with the hands going first. Nobody has ever managed to describe it. I am going to try, because it is the middle of the night and the middle of the book, and because I have finally understood what it is, and I need to say it before I lose it.

You think you are playing. For a while you are — you are choosing, you are listening to what you just did and deciding what to do next, there is a man at the piano and he is in charge. And then, somewhere, without a line you could point to, the hands get ahead of him. They go to the next thing before he has decided it. Then the thing after. And the man who was in charge finds that he is standing a little behind his own hands, watching them, the way you watch a good dog work a field: they do not need him, and it would be a mistake to whistle.
So he stops interfering.

And this is the part nobody manages to describe. The man goes quiet. Not the hands — the man. The part of you that is always saying I am doing this, I am here, how am I doing, what do they think — that part, which has been talking since you woke up this morning and has been talking all your life, stops talking. It does not go to sleep. It just has nothing to say, because there is no longer an I in the room to say it about. There are hands and there is music and there are a hundred people breathing, and the hands are going where the music is going, and the man is not there.
Where is he? I have thought about this for forty years. I do not know. Somewhere just behind, just to the side, in a place with no clock in it.

Because time is the second thing to go. I will play what I am told afterwards was twenty minutes and it was no time at all, and I will play what I am told was one minute and it was an afternoon. And when I come up — because you do come up, the way a swimmer comes up, with a kind of surprise at the air — I cannot tell you what I played in the middle. I know I began. I know I ended. The middle is a place I was, and cannot describe, and did not keep.

Here is what the doctors say about it, in plain words, because I asked them once, in another connection, and because I am going to need you to have it. When a person is deep in a skill — a surgeon, a runner, a man at a piano — the part of the brain at the front, the part that watches and judges and keeps track of the self, goes quiet. It can be measured. It dims, like a light on a board. Everything the hands need is lower down and further back, in the old parts, and those get brighter, and the watcher at the front simply steps out of the way because it would only slow things down. That is all it is. It is not holy. It is the body deciding, for an hour, that it does not need you.
And the strange thing — the thing I was told and did not believe until I watched for it — is where the pleasure is.

You would think the pleasure is in the arriving. The chord lands, the phrase comes home, the room sighs. But it is not there, not for the one playing. For the one playing the pleasure comes just before — a bar before, half a bar — in the knowing-what-is-coming, in the hands already going there while the room does not yet know. The body gives you the reward for the promise, not for the keeping of it. So I feel the thing a moment before they do, and by the time it reaches them and they weep, I am already past it and feeling the next one. I enjoy it, if that is the word. I enjoy it a bar early and I enjoy it alone and I cannot hold onto it, because the moment I try to hold it the man comes back into the room and the hands stop being ahead and it is gone.
Presence. Without memory.
I am going to say that again because I have just understood it, with the third year going by in lights and the violin a half-step behind me and a hundred people breathing in the dark.

For forty years I have gone, every night I have played well, to a place where I am entirely here and keep nothing. Where the hands know and the man does not. Where there is no past and no future and no self to carry either, only this, only now, only the next note arriving and being gone. I have called it the best thing in my life. I have built a room so I could go there nightly.
And my mother lives there.

She has lived there for six years. She is there now, in her chair behind me, with her eyes following the lights. She is entirely present and keeps nothing. Her hands know things her head does not. There is no past in her and no future and only a very small self left to miss them, and in the care home when she played four minutes without a wrong note and turned to me and asked if I wanted the room, she was not somewhere terrible. She was where I go. She was in the zone, and she could not come out, and I had spent forty years trying to get in.
The same country.

I have been visiting her every night without knowing it. Every night I have sat down at this piano and gone to where she is and played for ninety minutes and come up and gone home and not understood that I had been with her. Not beside her. With her. In the one place where neither of us has a name.

I come up now. I have no idea what I just played. The lights are going down over the water in handfuls and the violin is finishing something I must have started, gently, like a person closing a door on a sleeping child.
Behind me, I hear my mother breathing. Slow, with the small catch at the top.

I lift my hands. I am shaking. I am not shaking. Both. I turn on the bench and look at her, and she is looking at the lights going down, with her head to one side, perfectly content, and I think: I know where you are. I have been there. It is all right there. It is better than all right.
And then I think the other thing, which I will not say yet.
I turn back to the keys. The third year.
12. THE LATE TUNE
It happens in the third year and I do not mean to do it.

I am coming back through the fragments and the hands are ahead of me again — a little; I am watching them; I have not gone all the way back under — and they finish one of hers, a short one, a Tuesday, four bulbs to the right going down, and in the dark between that one and the next they do not wait for me.
They go on.

Something slow. Four notes going up, one at a time, with a rest between each as if somebody were climbing stairs and stopping on every step. Then a turn at the top. Then down, but not the way they went up — the way down is softer and goes further, below where it started, and settles there on a low note the way a person settles into a chair.
It is beautiful. I say that without pride because I did not choose it. It is the most beautiful thing that has been played in the room tonight and I do not know what it is.
And nothing lights.

I keep my hands on it — they are still going, into a second line now, the same four stairs and the same turn but changed a little, the way a mother changes a thing the second time she sings it — and I look up at the room and the room is dark. Not the between-dark, the breath between two fragments. Dark all the way down. Two thousand bulbs standing in the water on their stems and not one of them answering.
My first thought is that the box has failed.

That is the engineer in me and it is a fair thought; the box has failed twice in two thousand nights and both times it was a cable. I look toward the stage edge where the small green light would be if the box were listening, and the small green light is there. The box is listening. It hears the tune. It has heard every tune I have played tonight and answered each one with the right bulb from among two thousand, and now it hears this one and says, as plainly as a machine can say anything: I do not know this.
The hands go on into a third line.

I should stop. I know I should stop. The whole room has gone still in a different way — not the held breath of the fiftieth minute but something more careful, a hundred people who have learned over an hour that light follows sound and are now sitting in sound with no light, and do not know what it means, and are waiting to be told. Behind me the violin has not come in. She does not know it either. The cello holds one low note, uncertain, like a hand put out in the dark.
And the saxophone — I hear him stand.
He does not play. He stands, with the instrument across him, and I know without turning that he is looking at her.
Because she has made a sound.

Under my hands, under the cello, in the dark, from the chair behind me, a sound I have not heard in six years of kitchens and will not pretend to describe except to say that it is the sound a person makes when her name is called from another room. Not a word. A turning. The breath catching on the way in and coming out as something very nearly a note.
I stop playing. The hands stop because I make them. The low note settles and dies.
I turn on the bench.

My mother’s face has changed. I have watched that face for six years change in only one direction — toward smooth, toward sand with the tide gone out — and it has changed the other way. Something has come up into it. Her eyes are not following lights, because there are no lights. They are open very wide and they are looking at nothing, at the dark over the water, the way you look when you are listening to something far off and are not sure yet whether you heard it.
Her mouth is open. Her lips are moving. And this time there is breath in it.

Two syllables. The same soft sound twice. And then — I lean toward her, over the keys, so far that the bench tips — and then the four stairs going up. In her voice. In no voice, in the thread of a voice she has had for six years, but the four stairs, and the turn at the top, and the start of the way down.
She is humming what I just played.

Or I just played what she has been humming. I do not know which way round it goes. I have never known which way round it goes, since I was eight years old at a piano in a north room with a dish being put down carefully in a kitchen two doors away.
