The woman beside her has taken her hand off my mother’s shoulder.

That is the thing I see last and should have seen first. For the whole night the hand has been there, and now it is not; it is pressed flat against the woman’s own mouth, and above it her eyes are on me, and they are wet, and she is shaking her head, very slightly, side to side, not no — something else. The way you shake your head at a thing you have waited for and did not think would come.
I turn back to the keys because I do not know what else to do with my face.
I play one of hers. A real one, a Thursday, five bulbs on the left. The lights come up. The room breathes out, relieved, as if a thing had been put right. The violin comes in, gratefully. We go on.
Behind me, very quietly, for the length of five bulbs, my mother goes on humming the four stairs. Then she stops where her attention goes somewhere else, and does not start again.
I have played in this room two thousand nights and I have just learned there is a tune the room does not know.
13. THE COURTYARD
I am going to tell you what happened in the courtyard. Once. Plainly. The way my father should have and could not.

I was not there. I was not born. Everything here came to me in pieces across a lifetime — from my father’s eleven words, from an aunt who drank, from a cousin who should not have been told and told me, from my mother herself in the end, in the only way she could — and I have put the pieces together the way you put a plate back together, and I am not going to pretend the cracks are not there.
It was summer. It was afternoon. It was the hottest part of the day, when the whole city lies down.

My mother was thirty-four. She had been a pianist since she was six and had played in halls, real ones, in a city that had them then, and she had married my father and had a son and had stopped playing in halls and had not stopped playing. There was a piano in the north room. She played every afternoon while the boy slept.
The boy was two.

He slept in the room on the east side of the courtyard, across from the north room, with the shutters closed against the heat and the door onto the courtyard pulled to. Not shut. Pulled to. Open a hand’s width, the way you leave a child’s door so you can hear him. My mother pulled the north room door to as well, so that the piano would not wake him. She had done this every afternoon of his life. Two doors, each a hand’s width open, and between them the courtyard with the pool in it, full, blue-tiled, waist-deep on a man and over the head of a two-year-old, with the tap at one end and the drain at the other and a rim of stone wide enough to sit on.
The pool was not covered. Nobody covered pools then. It was where you washed the fruit.
She played. I know what she played, because she hummed it for fifty years. Four notes going up like stairs. A turn at the top. A softer way down that goes further than it came, and settles.

It was an old piece, nobody famous — the kind every girl at the conservatory in that city was given in her second year, and the kind every piano teacher in the world hands a child in his second year, which is how it came to me at eight and how her thread and my piece met in a house. That is the whole of the coincidence, and it was enough. She loved it the way you love a thing you have played a thousand times, which is to say she could play it without being there, and she was not there. She was where I go. She was in the zone, with the shutters closed and the door pulled to and the heat lying on the courtyard like a cloth, and the hands were ahead of her, and the woman had gone quiet.
He woke.

I do not know why. Children wake. He got down from the bed — he was two; he could get down from a bed — and he went to the door that was open a hand’s width and he went through it into the courtyard, into the light, in his vest, barefoot on hot stone, and the piano was going in the north room, the sound he had gone to sleep to every afternoon of his life, and he did what a child does. He went toward it.
Between him and it was the pool.
She finished the piece.

That is the sentence. That is the one my father could not say and my aunt could only say drunk and my cousin should never have known. She finished the piece, and it was so good — it had gone so well, the hands so far ahead, the woman so far gone — that she did what a pianist does when a thing has gone that well.
She played it again.

Four minutes. Perhaps five. The same four stairs, the same turn, the same way down. And in the courtyard, in the full afternoon light, in a pool where you washed the fruit, something that had made very little noise — a two-year-old makes almost none in water; they tell you that now; nobody told her — was finished, and lay still, and the piano went on in the north room through the door that was pulled to, going down the soft way, and settling.
She came up. The way a swimmer comes up. With a kind of surprise at the air.

She lifted her hands and held them a moment, the way you do, and put them in her lap, and sat in the north room with the sweat on her and the silence after a thing played well, and she heard — I have thought about this more than about anything else in my life — she heard that the courtyard was quiet.
Not the quiet of a child asleep. The other quiet.
She went to the door.

I am not going to tell you what she saw. I am not going to tell you what she did, or the sound she made, or what my father found when he came home at six to a silence in the courtyard and a woman sitting on the stone rim of a pool with her feet in the water and her hands held out in front of her as if they belonged to someone else. You know. You have known since the tarp. I am not going to make you look at it any longer than she did.
I will tell you three things.

She never played again. Not that night, not that year, not for fifty years, not in the north room, not in any house in any country — the back of a hand on the keys in a school hall, once, and four minutes in a lounge full of plastic flowers at the very end, and nothing else. The piano stayed under its sheet until my father bought me one and then she could not look at the new one either. Her hands had done something while she was not there to stop them, and she would not give them the chance again. That is the first thing.

The second is that she hummed. From the first week. My father told my aunt, who told me, that it began at the funeral — a thread of sound coming out of her, under her breath, going up four steps and turning and starting down and stopping. He thought it would pass. It did not pass for fifty years. She hummed because humming has no hands. She hummed the piece she had played twice, over and over, every day, and never once finished it, because the finishing was the thing.
The third thing is me.

They covered the pool. They did not drain it, which I have never understood and have stopped trying to; they put a green canvas over it and pegged it at the corners and left the water underneath, and the next year I was born, and I grew up riding a tricycle round a grave with rain on it, and I learned the piano in the north room with the door open, and my mother stood in the doorway and looked at the rug, and I thought it was a game.
You finished it, she said to me, at eleven, with the back of her hand on the keys.

I did. I had played the four stairs and the turn and the soft way down, and I had gone all the way to the end and stopped, and taken my hands off, and nothing in the world had happened. No door. No quiet. Just a hall clapping, and a small woman in a dark coat coming up three steps to touch the keys the way you check a child for fever.
I thought she was proud of me.

She was. That is the part I did not understand until I had a child of my own. She was proud of me, and she was telling me — the only way she could, in a school hall, in front of strangers — that it was all right to finish. That the thing she could not do, I could. That the song could be finished and the world would still be there at the end of it.
I have finished a great many songs since then. I built a room to finish them in. I have never once got to the end of one without, for a half-second, listening for the courtyard.
14. WHAT SHE KNOWS
I stand up.

I have never done that in the middle of a night. The hands are tired and the man is back in the room and I need, for one minute, to not be at a piano. I nod to the cello and he understands and puts down a long low note and holds it, and the violin lays a thin line over it, and together they make a kind of floor for the room to stand on while I am gone. The lights stay dark. The hundred breathe. Nobody minds. They think it is part of it. Perhaps it is.
I go to my mother.

Three steps. I crouch beside her chair so that my face is at the height of hers, and I take her hand out of her lap, and it is warm and small and the skin of it moves over the bones the way an old woman’s does, and she lets me, and looks at me, pleasantly, as at a stranger who has been kind.
“Maman,” I say. Mother. It is the one word of the old language I have never been able to give up.
She smiles. She does not know me. She has not known me for two years. But she smiles at the word the way you smile at a bell.
“Did you hear it?” I say. I am not sure what I am asking. “Just now. The one that — the room didn’t know it. Did you hear it?”
She goes on smiling. Her eyes go past me to the dark where the lights were.
And the woman beside her says, very low, so that it is only for the three of us: “She knows it.”
I look up.

I have told you about this woman in pieces, because that is how I see her — the hand on the shoulder, the eyes on me, the key to the house and the list of the tablets — and I am going to tell you now that crouched at my mother’s chair in the dark with the cello holding the floor up, I look at her face properly for the first time tonight, and I cannot, for a moment, think who she is.

I know her. Of course I know her. She has been in every room my mother has been in for two years. But her face in the half-dark is a face I know from somewhere else, somewhere further back, and I cannot put my hand on it, and it frightens me, the way it frightens you when a word you have said all your life suddenly looks wrong written down.
Then it passes, and she is the woman who looks after my mother, and she has said she knows it.
“Knows what?”

“The one you played. The slow one. The stairs.” She says it the way I would. She has been listening to me talk about this room for a long time. “She knows it. She’s always known it. You’ve just never played it in here before.”
“I’ve never played it anywhere,” I say. “I don’t know it. My hands —“ and I stop, because my hands did it without me is not a thing you say to a person about a piano, even in this room.
She is quiet for a moment. The cello holds. Somewhere in the hundred a person coughs and is ashamed of it.
“It’s a lullaby,” she says.
I look at my mother. My mother is looking at the dark.

“It’s the thing she hummed,” the woman says. “All those years. The four notes going up. It’s a lullaby. It has words. She sang it with the words once — only once, that I know of — in the kitchen, near the end, and you were there.”
“I don’t remember that.”
“No,” she says, and something goes across her face that I cannot read in the dark. “No. You wouldn’t.”

The violin has run out of line and begins another. I am aware that I have been away from the piano for a long time, for this room. I am aware that I am crouched on a stage in front of a hundred people holding my mother’s hand and that my legs have begun to hurt. I do not get up.
“Who was it for?” I say.

I know. I have known since I was fourteen in a chair in a courtyard with a boy and the water and the word enough in my lap. I ask anyway, because I have never once in my life heard anyone say it out loud, and I am sixty — forty-five — I am a grown man with a child of my own and I want, once, before the night is over, to hear somebody say it.
“For the boy,” she says. “The one before you. She wrote it for him. After.”
After.

“She never sang it to him,” the woman says. “She couldn’t have. She wrote it after. It’s not a lullaby to put a child to sleep. It’s a lullaby to —“ and she stops, and I watch her decide how to say it to a man crouched at his mother’s chair, and she chooses, the way my father chose, and says it plainly. “It’s for a child who’s already asleep. It’s what she had instead of saying sorry.”
My mother’s hand is warm in mine. She has begun, very softly, to hum. Not the stairs. Something else, a Tuesday, going nowhere.
“You know all this,” I say. “How do you know all this.”
And the woman looks at me, and I see it again — the face from further back, the one I cannot put my hand on — and she says, gently, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world:
“You told me. You tell me every night.”

I let go of my mother’s hand. I stand, and my knees say what they think about it, and I go back to the piano and sit, and the cello lets the floor down and the violin finishes her line, and I put my hands on the keys.
They are cold. First time tonight. Two strangers meeting.
I warm them on the cup. Full. I put it down.
15. THE ONE WITH NO BULB
I play it on purpose.

I have never done that either. Two thousand nights and I have never once chosen a thing to play in this room; I have let the hands go and the box answer and called it honest. Tonight I have chosen the order, and now I choose a tune, and I sit for a moment with my hands over the keys knowing exactly what I am going to do, which is the loneliest a pianist ever is.
Four notes going up. One at a time, with the rest between, like stairs.

I play them slowly. I give each one its own light to not have. The room has learned by now — a hundred people who could not have told you an hour ago what a filament was have learned that this room answers, and they wait for the answer, and I feel them wait. The first note: dark. The second: dark. By the third I hear them understand, a small shift in the breathing across eleven platforms, the sound of a hundred people realising they are being shown something and not told what.
The turn at the top.

The violin comes in under it this time. She has it now; she heard it in the third year and she heard my mother and she has been waiting for me to go back, and she lays a thin line under the turn, and the cello finds the low note that the way down is going to settle on and puts it there early, waiting, like a hand under a falling thing.
The way down. Softer. Further than it came.

Dark. Two thousand bulbs standing in the water and not one of them lit, and the water under them black and still, and the music going on over it, the most beautiful thing played in this room tonight, and the room saying, patiently, for the second time: I do not know this.
And I understand.
Not all of it. Not yet. But the engineer in me understands, with the hands going on into the second line, and I want to give it to you now, plainly, because it is simple and because it matters.

The box knows what it was given. That is all a box can know. For six years I put a telephone on a counter and I caught what my mother hummed over it, thousands of times, and every one of those is in there, married to a bulb, waiting to be called. And she hummed this. She hummed this more than anything — the woman beside her is right; she hummed it every day for fifty years, the four stairs and the turn and the start of the way down — and yet it is not in the box.
Because she never finished it.

That is what the box holds. The pieces. The start of the stairs and the stop. Three notes and her attention going somewhere else. Two notes. One. I have thousands of fragments of this tune in there, each married to its own bulb, and not one of them is this — the whole thing, the way down, the settling. The box has never heard it whole. She never let it. She stopped before the end every time for fifty years because the end was the thing she could not go to, and so the end was never recorded, and so the tune, whole, has no bulb.
I am playing the one thing of hers I never caught.

My hands have it anyway. I do not know how. I learned it once, at eight, and have not played the slow piece since I was eleven in a hall; and yet the hands have the whole of it, the way down and the settling, as if they had been keeping it for me in the dark the way the box keeps the rest.
I think — and this is a thought I have been keeping under the other one — I think: she sang it once. With the words. In the kitchen. Near the end. And I was there.
And I do not remember.

A thing happened in a kitchen, to me, with my mother, that a woman I cannot quite place says I was present for, and it is gone. Not faded. Gone. The way the film was gone from the people in the hospital room who were still sad. And I am sitting at a piano playing the thing the film left behind, perfectly, with no memory of the film.
I finish it. All the way. The soft way down, further than it came, and the low note, and the settling, and I take my hands off, and hold them a moment in the air, the way you do.
Nothing in the world happens. No door. Just dark, and water, and a hundred people not breathing.
Behind me my mother says, quite clearly, in a voice I have not heard from her in two years — her own voice, the one from before, the one that said you finished it into my hair in a school hall:
“There.”
Just that. The way you say it when a thing has been put where it belongs.
Then the lights.

Not from me. I have not touched the keys. From the far end of the room, one bulb comes up — the last one, the one I put as far from the stage as the room goes, the Thursday, the single held note — and goes down. And then another, nearer. And another. The box is doing something I did not build it to do: it is going back through them — every fragment I have played tonight and others I have not — one bulb after another coming up and going down across the marsh in a slow wave from the back of the room toward the stage, as if the room were remembering the evening for itself.
I turn to the stage edge. The green light is on. The box is not listening to me.
It is listening to her.

She is humming. Not the stairs. The small ones. The Tuesdays. One after another, in no order I can hear, the fragments of her last six years coming out of her in the dark the way they came out over a counter, and the box hears each one and knows it and lights it — not one bulb; a dozen, twenty, every bulb that ever held that shape

— and she leaves no gap between them for the box to let go in, and the room is filling with light from the back forward like a town waking up street by street, and the hundred have stopped breathing entirely, and the violin has put down her bow.

I do not play. There is nothing for me to do. I sit at a dark piano with my hands in my lap and watch two thousand bulbs light one at a time to the sound of my mother humming, and I think — I cannot help it; it is the engineer — I did not record this. This is not in the box. She is humming now and the box is lighting what she hummed then and I do not know how it is telling the difference.
It is not. It is not telling the difference, because there is none. She is humming exactly what she hummed. She has never hummed anything else.

The wave reaches the stage. The last bulbs come up, the nearest ones, the ones from the first year, and the whole room is lit, every stem, two thousand small gold lights standing in the water and two thousand more under it, and in the light I can see every face on every platform turned toward a small woman in a chair with a blanket on her knees, and I can see the woman beside her, who has put her hand back on my mother’s shoulder, and is not looking at me for once.
She is looking at my mother. Her face is wet and it is doing a thing I have no word for.

Then my mother stops, where her attention goes somewhere else, and the room goes down. All of it, together, slowly, gold to orange to the red thread you can only see if you know where to look, and then dark.
The water moves.
In the dark, I count. I am an engineer; I count. Two thousand one hundred and forty bulbs, and all of them lit, and one tune that never had one.
I put my hands on the keys. They are warm. I do not know whose.
INTERLUDE THREE — THE ROOM
He thinks there is one kind of forgetting. He has read every book a man can read and he thinks there is one kind, and it is hers, and it comes in like a tide over a riverbed and takes from the top.
There is another kind.

I am not going to say whose it is. Not yet. In here nothing has a name until it is called. But I have had a year of nights, and I have watched a man come across the water every one of them, and I know a thing about the other kind that he does not, and you should have it now, before the room is dark again and there is nowhere left to put it.
The other kind does not come in like a tide. It comes in like weather.

It is here, and then it is gone, and then it is here. A person can be entirely himself at six o’clock and gone by seven, and back by nine with no idea he was away. The doctors call this fluctuating. The word means it goes up and down. The people who live with it have a better word. They say: he’s in or he’s out. Like the tide, but not a tide you can set a clock by. A tide that comes when it likes.
The other kind shows you things.

Not frightening things, usually. People. Children, often. An animal in the corner of a room. They are very clear and very quiet and they do not do anything; they sit, they watch, they are simply there, where nothing is. The person seeing them often knows they are not real and is not troubled by them. He may grow fond of them. He may stop mentioning them, because he has learned what happens to the faces of people he mentions them to.
The other kind takes the body.

Slowly. A stiffness. A tremor in the hands when they are still. A shuffle that was not there last year. The same thing, in fact, that takes a different set of people under a different name — the one everybody has heard of, the one that shakes. The same bad protein, in a different room of the brain. And here is the one mercy in it, and it is real, and the doctors will tell you so: music steadies it. A man who cannot walk across a kitchen can walk to a beat. Hands that shake in a lap are still on a keyboard. The body that cannot be trusted alone can be trusted with a tune. Nobody fully knows why.
The other kind is faster. Years, not a decade.

And the other kind — this is the thing I most want you to hold — does not take the memories first. It leaves them where they are, in their layers, for a long time. What it takes is the way in. The memory is on the shelf; the ladder is gone. A thing can be there, whole, and the man cannot reach it — until something reaches it for him. A smell. A hand on his shoulder. A tune.
A woman’s voice, saying a thing she has said before.
Here is the third verse. He has heard it now, whole, in his own hands, and the room stayed dark for it, and he thinks he understands why. He understands half.
Laa-laa, laa-laa — I did not hear the door.
The line that I loved was so beautiful that I played it once more.
When I came through at last, the moon had gone out of its place, and the water had taken a small thing instead, and had closed over its face.
IV. DARK
16. THE MAP
I know every bulb. I have told you that. Here is how, in the second year, with the fragments long and the marsh more light than dark, it stopped being true.

I am into the second year. The fragments are long now, eight seconds, ten, the ones with shape in them, and the bulbs come up in handfuls near the stage and the whole marsh is more light than dark and the violin and the cello are carrying each phrase further than I take it, and the man is back in the room — I have not gone under again since the stairs — and so I am watching, and counting, and I am doing the thing I do on good nights, which is naming them.

That one. The Tuesday. Eleven seconds, something almost whole, and my father’s name said clearly into a kitchen as if he had just come in. I know that bulb. Left of the stage, low, third stem from the walkway.

I play it. Nine bulbs come up — but not that one. Not the low one, third from the walkway. The low one stays dark and a bulb I did not expect comes up far to the right, high, and I look at it and think: no. That’s wrong. That’s the Thursday with the tap running.
I play on. I tell myself I was mistaken. A man can be mistaken about a bulb.
Then she asks me.

The woman. She leans forward in the dark behind my mother’s chair and says, quite quietly, not to interrupt, in the tone of a person who has been wanting to ask something all night and has decided this is the moment: “Which one is it? The one where she says his name. You always say you could take someone to it.”
And I open my mouth to tell her, and I cannot.

I know I know. That is the feeling, exactly — I know that I know, the way you know a word is in your mouth. Left of the stage. Low. Third from the walkway. I look at the third stem from the walkway and it is a stem like the others, with a dark bulb on it like the others, and I cannot say whether the Tuesday is there or whether the Tuesday is the high one to the right that lit when it should not have, or whether I have ever known where the Tuesday was, or only said so.
“I —“ I say.
I play something else to cover it. The room lights. The woman sits back. She does not ask again. I feel her not asking.
And I am going to tell you what I have not told anyone, because the hands are going on without me and I have nothing else to do with the man while they do.

Two years ago the box failed. Not the box — the file in it, the one that said which recording was married to which bulb. The list. The map. Six years of a kitchen cut into thousands of pieces and every piece given a number and every number given a stem, and the file that held all of that went, the way files go, in an afternoon, for no reason anyone could find, and when the room came back on that night every bulb was still wired to a recording but I no longer knew which.

I rebuilt it. I sat in this room alone for three weeks with the recordings and played each one and watched which bulb answered and wrote it down. Two thousand one hundred and forty times. I made a new map.

Here is the thing I did not tell anyone. The new map is not the old one. It cannot be. The old one was made from the kitchen — I knew, when I married the Tuesday to the low stem third from the walkway, that it was the Tuesday, because I had cut it from the recording myself that week with the date on it and my father’s name in the middle of it. The new map was made from the room. I played a sound and watched a light. I knew which light; I did not know which Tuesday. The dates were gone. The names of the days were gone. What I had was two thousand pieces of a woman humming and two thousand stems, and I matched them the way you match socks in the dark, by feel, and told myself it was the same.
It is not the same.

I have been standing at the door of this room for two years telling a hundred strangers a night that it is a map. That I could take them to the one where she says his name. That there is a bulb for the Thursday in the second year and I know which. I have believed it while I said it. That is the thing about a lie you tell every night; it goes in the box with the rest.

It is not a map. It was never a map, not since the file went, and perhaps not before. It is weather. Thousands of pieces of her coming and going over black water in an order I do not control and cannot name, lighting where they light, and the man at the piano who says he knows which is which is the only person in the room who does not know that he does not know.
The hands finish the second year. The room goes down in handfuls.
I sit in the dark between and I feel — I want to be exact — I feel relieved.

That is the first honest thing the room has done for me, I think. It has taken the map out of my hands. For two thousand nights I have sat here as the man who knew where everything was, and tonight, with a woman’s question hanging in the dark behind me and a Tuesday that lit in the wrong place, I am as lost in this room as any stranger on any platform, and the lights are coming and going for me the way they come and go for them, and I do not know where my mother is in here, and it is beautiful, and I am nobody in it.
I lift my hands. The first year is next. The longest fragments. The ones that nearly went somewhere.
I look up before I start, to find the far wall in the dark, the way I always do, to fix where I am.
And there is a boy sitting on the last platform.
17. THE CHILD ON THE WATER
He is on the platform furthest from the stage, the eleventh, where the single held note has its bulb — the one I put as far away as the room goes.

He is sitting on the edge of it with his feet over the water. Not in the water. Over it, hanging, the way a child sits on a wall. He is small. Two, perhaps three. He is wearing something pale — a vest, I think, the kind children slept in once in hot countries — and nothing on his feet, and his hands are flat on the wood either side of him, and he is looking at the piano.
At me.

I want to tell you I was afraid. I was not. And I think it is the most important thing about the whole of that minute: that I looked across a flooded warehouse in the near-dark and saw a two-year-old sitting with his feet over black water where no child could be, and what I felt was not fear and not even surprise but something nearer to oh — there you are. The way you feel when a person you have been expecting all evening finally comes in, and you had stopped watching the door.

He is very still. Children that age are never that still. He does not swing his feet. He does not look round at the hundred people on the platforms around him, who do not seem to see him, whose faces are all turned toward the stage. He looks at the piano with his head a little to one side, the way my mother looks at things now, as if everything had just arrived and he had not been told what any of it was for.
I do not look away from him. I play.

The first year. The long ones. I give him the longest fragment I have — fourteen seconds, from the first month, the kitchen in the valley before anything had really gone, my mother humming something with a beginning and a middle and very nearly an end, something you could call a tune and not be lying — and a dozen bulbs come up together near the stage, and in their light I look across the room and he is still there, lit faintly now from the front, the pale vest, the small hands.
He has not moved. But his face has changed. He is listening.
Of course he is. He went to sleep to it every afternoon of his life.
I am going to say now what I did not say in the zone, the thing underneath, because he is sitting across the water from me and there is no longer any reason not to.

I have known about him my whole life. Since before the tarp, since the green canvas was the floor of the courtyard and I did not know a floor could be a question. He has been in every room I have ever played in. Not seen — I have never seen him, not once, not until this minute — but there, in the half-second at the end of every song when I listen for the courtyard. He is the reason I listen. He is the reason my mother stood in doorways. He is the four stairs and the turn and the way down that nobody finished for fifty years, and I have built a room of two thousand lights over black water and I have not once, until now, let myself say what the water was.

It is the pool. Of course it is. I flooded a floor a hand’s depth and stood a piano in the middle of it and asked a hundred people a night to sit above it and not get wet. I told them the water was for the light. I told myself that.
He is sitting with his feet over it. He is not afraid of it either.

I play the first year. Fragment after fragment, the long ones, the hopeful ones, and the room is as bright as it gets — a town at full evening, every street lit, the water underneath a second town trembling — and the violin and cello and now the saxophone are carrying each phrase on past me like people passing a thing hand to hand down a line, and the hundred have stopped weeping and are simply looking, with their faces open, the way people look at a thing too large to have feelings about yet.
And across all of it a small boy sits on the far platform and listens to his mother hum.

I do not tell anyone. I understand — some part of me, the engineer, the part that has read the books — I understand what happens to the faces of people you tell this to. I have seen it happen to my own face in a mirror once, in a doctor’s office. So I do not turn to the woman behind me and say do you see him. I play. I give him the first year. I give him his mother at her best, before I was born, when she still nearly finished things.
Near the end of it he looks away from me for the first time.

He looks at the water under his feet. He looks at it for a long moment, the way children look at water, with interest and no fear. Then he looks back at the stage — not at me this time; past me, at the chair behind me — and his face does the thing a child’s face does when it finds the one it was looking for in a crowd.
I do not turn round. I know who is behind me.

The first year ends. I am at the bottom of the house. Everything I have of her is played, except the thing that has no bulb, and the room goes down in a slow wave from the far edges inward, street by street, the nearest lights last.
In the last of it he is still sitting there. Then it is dark, and I cannot see him, and I do not know if he is there.

I put my hands in my lap. I have played every fragment of my mother that was ever caught, in order, from the last to the first, and I am empty, and there are ten minutes left, and I do not know what they are for.
18. NOT MY MOTHER
There are ten minutes left and I have played everything, and I turn on the bench, in the dark, to look at my mother.
I have to tell this exactly. I owe it exactly, to her, to the woman, to you.

There is one light in the room. Not a bulb — the small green light at the edge of the stage that says the box is listening. By it I can see the chair behind the bench, and the shape of a woman in it, and the pale of her face, and her hands in her lap.
One woman.

I look for the other. I look for my mother’s blanket and my mother’s white hair cut short by someone kind and my mother’s smooth face with the tide gone out of it, and I look for the woman standing beside her with the hand on her shoulder, and in the green light there is one chair and one woman in it, and her hair is dark, and her face is not smooth. It is a face in its late thirties with a line between the brows that has been there, I think, for about a year, and her eyes are on me, and they are wet, and she is not looking after anyone. She is sitting alone.
“Where is she,” I say.
The woman does not answer at once.
“Where’s my mother. She was here. You had your hand on her.” I hear my voice and it is not steady and I do not care. “What have you done with her.”
“Dad,” the woman says.

I do not know why she says that. It is the wrong word. It is a word from a different sentence, from somebody else’s night, and it goes past me like a car going the wrong way down a street. I stand up. The hundred breathe behind me; I have forgotten them. The cello, bless him, puts down a long low note so that the room has something to stand on, and I walk the three steps to the chair and I look down at the woman in it.

I know her. I have told you that. Her face is from somewhere further back and I cannot put my hand on it and tonight it does not frighten me any more, it makes me angry, because she is sitting in my mother’s chair and my mother is not in the room.
“You are not my mother,” I say.

I say it quite politely. I want that understood. I am not a man who raises his voice and I do not raise it now; I say it the way you would say it to a stranger who had sat down at your table in a café, courteously, with the firmness of a man who happens to be right. “I’m sorry. I don’t know who you are. But you’re not her. Someone has — you’ve been put here. You need to go and get her. Please. Go and fetch my mother.”
The woman looks up at me for a long moment.

I am going to tell you her face, because it is the thing in this whole book I most want you to have, and because I did not understand it for another ten minutes and you are going to understand it now.

It does not do what faces do when you say a thing like that to them. It does not flinch. It does not argue. It does not do the thing I have watched faces do in doctors’ offices, the careful arranging, the now then. It does something I have only ever seen one other face do, in a lounge full of plastic flowers, when a woman turned on a piano bench and asked a stranger if he wanted the room.
It accepts.
“All right,” she says.

And she stands up and touches my arm once, lightly, on the way past, the way you touch a railing, and she goes. Along the walkway, in the dark, without a lamp, as if she could do it with her eyes shut, and the small human door in the big black one opens and shows a line of yellow light and shuts again, and she is gone, and I am standing on a stage in the middle of a flooded warehouse beside an empty chair with a hundred people watching me and a cello holding one note under me and I have sent a woman out of the room to fetch my mother.
I stand there.

I do not know how long. The cello’s note is very long. The violin has not come in; she is watching me, I think, over the top of her instrument, and I do not look at her. I look at the empty chair, and at the dark where the lights were, and at the green light that says the box is listening to a room in which nobody is playing anything.
Then the door.

The line of yellow. The shape of a woman coming through it, and the door shutting, and her coming back along the walkway in the dark toward the stage, and up the step, and across to the chair, and sitting down in it, and putting her hands in her lap, and looking up at me.
And I say — I hear myself say it, with the whole of my chest going loose —
“There you are.”
She nods.

“Where did you go?” I say. “I was worried. There’s a woman —“ I look round for her, the other one, the one I sent, and the stage is empty but for the three young ones and the chair and us. “There was a woman here. She’d sat in your chair. I sent her to get you.”
“I know,” my mother says. “She found me.”

“Good.” I crouch beside the chair, the way I did before, and take her hand out of her lap, and it is warm, and the skin of it does not move over the bones the way an old woman’s does, it is smooth and young and the grip in it is strong, and I notice this and I put it where I put things I notice and cannot use. “Good. I didn’t like her. I don’t know who she was.”
“No,” my mother says. “You wouldn’t.”

I look at her. In the green light her face is wet and she is not wiping it. Her eyes are on mine and they are doing something I have no word for and it is not pity and it is not grief and I have seen it before, tonight, when the whole room lit to a woman humming, and I did not know then what it was either.
“Are you all right?” I say.
“Yes,” she says. “I’m all right. Play the last ten minutes. Then we’ll go home.”
I stand. My knees say what they think. I go to the piano and sit, and the cello lets his note go, and I warm my hands on the cup. Full. I put it down.

Behind me, very quietly, the way you say a thing to yourself in an empty house, I hear her say one more word. I do not know what it means. It is the word from the wrong sentence, the car going the wrong way, and it goes past me and is gone.
“Dad.”
19. THE WALL
There is a woman who lies awake. This is before the room.
She lies on her side in a bed in a house in the hills, in the dark, with her face toward the wall, and through the wall she listens to a piano.

There is no piano. She knows that. She has known it for years. The room on the other side of the wall has a bed in it and a chair and a window onto the garden and a man asleep, and the man’s hands are moving on the blanket, and that is the piano: the sound of two hands on cloth, going, in the dark, as if there were keys under them. She can hear the shape of it. Not notes — cloth does not make notes — but the rhythm, the rise and fall, the pauses where a pianist would breathe. She has heard it so many nights that she can tell, lying with her face to the wall, which piece it is.
Tonight it is the slow one. The stairs.

She does not go in. She learned not to, years ago, the first time, when she went in with her heart going and found him flat on his back with his eyes shut and his hands lifting and falling on the blanket and his face entirely at peace, and she said his name — the name she had always called him, which was not his name, which was Dad — and he did not wake, and the hands went on, and she understood that he was somewhere she could not follow and that he was happy there and that waking him would be a kind of theft.
So she lies with her face to the wall and listens to her father play in his sleep.

The doctors had a word for it. She looked it up afterwards, the way you do, in the kitchen at two in the morning with the laptop light on her face. People do it years before anything else shows. Decades, sometimes. They live their dreams with their bodies — shout, strike out, run in the bed — and it is one of the earliest signs there is of the thing that is coming, and almost nobody knows that, and so almost nobody is warned. Her father did not shout. Her father played. For eleven years, through a wall, every few nights, and she had thought it was sweet.
She thinks about the kitchen in the valley.

She was eleven the first time she saw the phone on the counter by the oranges. She asked what it was for and her father — Arman, to everyone but her; she has always liked being the one person who did not have to use it — said it’s for your grandmother and she did not understand and did not ask again, and the phone was on the counter every time they visited, for years, with its small red light, and her grandmother hummed over it and moved it to wipe the surface and put it back. She was sixteen when the humming went down to one note. She was seventeen when it stopped.
She was thirty-one when she put a phone on her own kitchen counter and pressed the red circle and left it there.

She did not plan it either. She had come down in the morning and her father was at the counter with an orange in his hand, turning it, the way you turn a thing to find where to start it, and he was humming. He had never hummed. In her whole life she had never once heard her father hum; he was a man who either played or was silent. And he was standing at her counter humming four notes going up like stairs, and a turn, and the start of a way down, and he stopped before the end, and said, “The — these. What do we call these,” and laughed.
She said the word. He said yes, of course, those. He peeled it. He hummed.
She went upstairs and sat on the edge of her bed for a long time with her hands between her knees. Then she came down and put the phone by the oranges.

Through the wall, the piano stops. The hands have come to the end of the stairs — not the end; the place before the end, the place where the piece turns and starts down — and stopped, the way they always stop, the way her grandmother always stopped, and there is quiet from the other room, and then the slow breathing of a man asleep.

She lies in the dark and thinks about the thing she is building. A warehouse. Water. The thousands of pieces of him she has caught at a counter in five years — she has not stopped; the phone is on the counter still — and the box she will put them in, and the bulbs. He thinks it is his. She has let him think it; it costs nothing, and some nights he remembers building the first one, the small one, years ago, for his mother, in a rented room with sixty-one strangers, and he tells her about it as if she had not been there, and she lets him.
She thinks: he will play, and the room will answer, and he will believe the lights are hers. And for a while it will be true enough.

She thinks: and then the lights will stop answering. Fewer each night. Because he will stop playing what he hummed, and start playing only what the hands know, and the hands know things the box was never given.
She thinks: and I will sit beside him while it happens, and he will call me by her name, and I will let him.
She turns onto her back. The ceiling. Through the wall, nothing. Then — faintly, cloth under two hands — the stairs begin again, from the bottom.

She does not sleep. She has not, properly, for a year. She lies and listens to her father almost finish something, over and over, through a wall, in a house in the hills, in a city where she was born and he was not, and she waits for morning, when he will come down and warm his hands on a cup he does not drink and look at her across the kitchen with a face that has not decided yet who she is.
20. THE REVERSAL
I put my hands on the keys.
They are old.
I promised you at the start that I would be a man you could trust. I have not been. This is the only way I know to put that right.

I look at them, in the green light, and they are an old man’s hands. I have looked at these hands every night of my life and they have been forty-five years old, the hands of a man halfway through, and tonight they are spotted on the backs and the knuckles are large and the skin over them is thin and loose and they are shaking. Not the shaking I know, the shaking of a man moved by something. A small fast steady tremor, in both hands, that stops the instant I lay them on the keys and starts again when I lift them.
I lift them. It starts. I lay them down. It stops.
I do this three times. The hundred wait. Behind me a woman I have just called my mother waits.

I think: I am sixty. And then, as if a hand had come down on the number and pushed it: I am seventy. I was born the year after the pool was covered and the pool has been covered seventy-two years and I have been doing that arithmetic all night and getting it wrong on purpose, the way you look past a thing in a room. A man of forty-five cannot have been born the year after a thing that happened seventy-two years ago. I have said both numbers tonight in the same breath and heard neither.

My mother is not eighty. My mother would be — I do the sum, and the sum is a hundred and six, and nobody’s mother is a hundred and six, and I understand, with my old hands flat on the keys and the tremor gone out of them, that my mother is dead.
She has been dead for twenty years.

I know when. I know the room — a window, a chair, a care home in the valley — and I know I was there and I know that she hummed, at the end, one note, and that I was holding her hand when she stopped, and that the hand was small and the skin moved over the bones. I have known this all night. I have known it for twenty years. I have been sitting at a piano telling a hundred strangers and you that she was in a chair behind me, and the knowing was on the shelf the whole time, whole, and the ladder was gone.
I turn, very slowly, on the bench.
One woman in one chair. Dark hair. Late thirties. A line between the brows. My daughter.
Laleh.

The name comes up out of the floor of me like a bulb at the back of a dark room. I do not say it. I cannot, yet. But I know it is there, the way I know the Tuesday is somewhere in the marsh, and I know that the hand that has been on my mother’s shoulder all night — always, the way you hold a railing — has been on nobody’s shoulder. It has been in her own lap. There has been one woman on this stage all night and I have seen two, because I needed two: the one I was playing for and the one who was keeping me.
The room shows people things. I know that. I have read every book a man can read, in another connection, in a doctor’s office, with my own face in a mirror doing the thing faces do.

And I understand, with the knowing in my lap, how much of what I have told you tonight was furniture I carried in from other rooms. The first night, the sixty-one, the woman in the yellow coat — that was a rented room, twenty-two years ago, and I have put it in this building because this is the only building I have. The map that failed, the three weeks alone rebuilding it — I do not know whose that was. Perhaps mine, in the old room. Perhaps nobody’s. Two thousand nights: this room has not had two thousand nights. I know that the way I know my own weight. I have been telling you the truth in the wrong order, from the wrong year, with the wrong woman in the chair, and every word of it was something that happened.
I look across the water. The eleventh platform is dark. I cannot see whether a boy is sitting on it, and I understand now why I was not afraid of him, and that it does not matter whether he is there.

I am seventy. I have a disease with a man’s name in it that comes and goes like weather and shows me children on the water and shakes my hands when they are still. My mother is twenty years dead. Someone has built me a room so that I can go every night to the one place where I am entirely here and keep nothing, and she sits behind me while I am there, and I call her by her grandmother’s name, and she lets me, and when I come up — because you do come up — she is there, and I do not know who she is, and she tells me.
Every night.

I have a few minutes of her left. The hands are on the keys and the tremor is gone and the man is in the room, entirely, for once, with the knowing all the way down off the shelf and in his lap, and I think, as clearly as I have thought anything in a year:
I am not going to be able to keep this.
Not the night. This. The minutes of knowing. It will go the way the film went, and I will be sad and not know why, and she will be in a chair and I will call her Maman, and she will say all right.
So I am going to use it.

I lift my hands from the keys and the shaking comes back and I let it. I turn on the bench, all the way round this time, and I look at my daughter, and she sees — I watch her see — that I am in. Her face does the thing. The one I have had no word for all night. I have a word for it now. It is what a face does when a person it has been waiting for all evening finally comes in, and it had stopped watching the door.
“Laleh,” I say.
INTERLUDE FOUR — THE ROOM
In here nothing has a name until it is called. He has called it. So I can say it now.

It is called Lewy body dementia. The first word is a man’s name — a doctor, a long time ago, who found the clumps under a microscope and did not know what they were for. The rest means what it says. It is the one most often called by the wrong name — as Parkinson’s, its cousin; as his mother’s disease; as something wrong in the mind of a man who has started seeing children in rooms. The doctors have a name for the moment he looked at his daughter and told her, courteously, that she was not his mother: the impostor feeling. It comes with this disease more than with any other. It is not cruelty. It is a face arriving without the place it belongs in.

You have had the rest of it already, with the third verse. Weather, not tide. People who are not there. The hands last, and steady only on the keys. The shelf with the ladder gone. I will not say it twice. He has had enough things said twice tonight.
Here is what I know that he does not, and that the daughter knows, and has known since the first month, and has not said.
Since the first month, fewer bulbs have lit each night.

Not because the box is failing. The box is perfect. She told you why, lying with her face to a wall. Every night the room is a little darker. Every night there is a little more music over the water that nothing answers. The hundred do not notice; each hundred comes once. She notices. She sits in the chair and counts, the way he used to, and the number goes down.

Tonight every bulb he played lit twice, and hundreds more he did not, because she hummed them. She knew that tonight was the last night, and she wanted him to see the room full once more, and she had learned his pieces in order to give them back to him, and did.
Tomorrow there is no room. The stems come out of the floor.
Here is the fourth verse. He knows now whose it is. It is his mother’s. It is also his.
Laa-laa, laa-laa — they told me the water was warm.
That it took you so gently you never once cried out for my arm.
I have put down the keys. I will hum, and I will not play — so that nothing I love will ever be louder than you, from this day.
V. WHAT STAYS
21. THE HOUR

She comes to me. I do not go to her; my knees have had enough of that tonight. She gets up out of the chair and crosses the three steps and crouches where I crouched, beside the bench, so that her face is at the height of mine, and she takes my hand out of my lap — it is shaking; she holds it until it is not — and she says, “Hello.”
“Hello,” I say.

That is how it goes, when I am in. I have learned that tonight and I think I have learned it before and lost it. There is no scene. Nobody weeps. Two people say hello to each other on a stage in the dark as if they had just met at a door, which they have.
“How long,” I say.
She knows what I am asking. She has had a year of me asking it.

“The room’s been open a year. You say two thousand nights; it’s three hundred and some. About a year since they said the name,” she says. “Longer before that. You were playing in your sleep for a long time before anyone knew what it was.”
“Through the wall.”
“Through the wall.”

I look at her. In the green light I can see the line between her brows and I want to put my thumb on it and smooth it like a page, and I do not, because I do not know whether I am allowed, because I do not know how many nights I have done it already and not known.
“Did I build this?” I say.
I know the answer. I am asking to hear it in her voice.

“No,” she says. “You built the first one. The small one, in the rented room, for her, the year before she stopped knowing rooms. Sixty-one people. You told me about it so many times that I could have built it from the telling.” She looks round at the dark marsh, the two thousand stems, the water. “So I did. Bigger. With you in the box instead of her.”
“Me.”

“You hum, Dad. You’ve hummed for six years. You stand at my counter with an orange in your hand and you hum the stairs and you stop before the end and you say what do we call these, and you laugh.” She says it gently, the way there was said behind me an hour ago. “You never used to. You told me once you were a man who played or was silent. I put the phone by the oranges the first morning I heard it. It’s still there.”
I look at the dark marsh. Thousands of stems. Thousands of pieces of a man at a counter.
“Then it was you humming. Before. When the whole room lit.”
“Yes. I know every one. I cut them myself. I wanted you to see it full once more.”
“Is it any good?”
She laughs. Once, surprised, the way the man did on the first night when he said that was my father. “Dad. A hundred strangers a night have cried in it for a year.”
“That’s not what I asked.”
“Yes,” she says. “It’s good. It’s the best thing I’ve ever made. I made it so you’d have somewhere to go.”
I think about that. The hands are quiet in hers.
“The boy,” I say.
She does not pretend not to understand. “On the far platform?”
“You’ve seen him?”
“No. You’ve told me. Most nights. You’re not frightened of him.”
“No,” I say. “I’m not. I thought I would be.”
“You said that too.”

I want to ask her a great many things and I can feel the hour — I know it is not an hour; I know it is minutes, that the weather is already turning at the edges, that in a little while the ladder will go and the shelf will still be there and I will look at this woman and see a stranger in my mother’s chair — I can feel it going and I want to use it well and I do not know what well is. So I ask the thing I have wanted to ask since the stairs.
“The lullaby. You said she sang it once. With the words. In the kitchen. And I was there.”
“Yes.”
“Tell me.”
She is quiet a moment. Behind her the cello has stopped and the room is simply dark and simply waiting, a hundred people who have learned that this room does what it does in its own time.

“It was near the end,” she says. “Her end. She’d stopped standing. You’d come in the morning to sit with her and I’d come after school, and that day I came in and you were both at her kitchen table — this was before the home — and she was singing. Not humming. Singing — words, low, that song, the stairs, all the way through. All the way down. The first time anyone had heard the end of it. And you were sitting across from her with your hands flat on the table, like this” — she puts my hand flat on my own knee — “and you were crying without any sound, the way you do. And when she finished she looked at you and said there, the way you’d say it when you put a thing down where it goes. And then she asked if you wanted the room.”
“I don’t remember that.”
“I know.”
“I don’t remember any of it.”
“I know, Dad. It’s all right. I do. That’s what I’m for.” She squeezes my hand once. “And your hands remember. You played it tonight. The whole thing. Twice. I’ve waited a year for that.”
I look at the keys.
“The box doesn’t know it,” I say.

“No. You never hummed the end. Not once. Six years at the counter and you stopped where she stopped, every time.” She smiles, and it is not a happy smile and it is not an unhappy one; it is the smile of somebody who has lived with a fact for a long time. “It’s the one thing of yours I couldn’t catch. So it’s the one thing in here with no bulb.”
“Good,” I say.
She looks at me.

“I mean it. Good. Let it have none.” I do not know quite what I mean and I say it anyway, because the weather is turning and I would rather say a true thing badly than nothing. “Everything else in here is a thing that was caught. That’s all right. That’s what the room is — a thing that answers when it’s called. But that one was never caught. It’s just in the hands. It’s the only thing in here that’s —“ and I cannot find the word, and she finds it for me.
“Present,” she says.
“Yes.”
“Without the other.”
“Yes.”
We stay like that. Her hand round mine, the two of us at the height of each other, in the green light, on a stage, with the water moving.
“There’s ten minutes,” she says eventually. “They paid for ninety. Do you want to stop?”
“No,” I say. “I want to play.”
“What?”
“I don’t know. Whatever the hands want. Nothing from the box.” I look at the dark marsh. “I’d like to play one set in here with nothing answering. I think I’ve wanted that for a long time.”
She nods. She stands and goes back to the chair, and sits, and puts her hands in her lap, and looks at me the way she has looked at me all night.
I warm my hands on the cup. Full. I put it down.

I feel the weather come in. It comes the way it comes — from the edges, the far platforms going first, the knowing going soft at the back like the far bulbs going down. I have perhaps a minute of her left. I use it to turn on the bench and say her name once more, so that it is the last thing the man says before he goes.
“Laleh.”
“I’m here.”
“Will you — if I don’t know you after —“
“I’ll tell you,” she says. “I tell you every night.”
I turn back to the keys. The man goes quiet. The hands go first.
22. THE LAST SET
I will not manage this. Nobody has. For once I am not going to tell you what I played, because I do not know, and that is the whole of it.
The hands go first.

Not to the box. Not to a Tuesday or a Thursday or anything with a bulb at the end of it. They go to a place in the keys I have not been tonight — lower, and slower — and they begin something, and I do not know what it is. It has the stairs in it somewhere. Four notes going up. But not at the start; somewhere inside, the way a face you know is somewhere inside a crowd.
Dark.

Of course dark. Nothing in the box knows this. The room, which has answered every sound I have made for ninety minutes and three hundred nights, hears this and says, patiently, kindly, for the last time: I do not know this. And I think — the man thinks, from just behind, just to the side, on his way out — no. Neither do I. Isn’t it beautiful.
The violin comes in.

She has nothing to follow. There is no fragment to carry further, no phrase to lay a line under. She listens for four bars and then she simply comes in beside me, a third above, not following, walking. The cello finds the floor of it and puts it there. And the saxophone — he stands, I hear him, the one who waits until it starts talking — plays with the reed barely touching, that closed private sound, and he does not take a tune from me, there is no tune to take; he hums. Over the water. In the dark. Like a woman in a kitchen two rooms away.
And the man is gone.

I want to be honest about this, since I have promised. I do not know what happened in the middle. I know I began — the low place in the keys, the stairs somewhere inside it — and I know I ended, because I came up, the way you come up, with a kind of surprise at the air. The middle is a place I was. I was entirely there. I kept nothing.
Here is what I can tell you, from the edges.

That the dark was complete. Two thousand bulbs standing in black water on their stems and not one of them lit, for ten minutes, and the music going over them, and a hundred people sitting in it who had stopped waiting for the light. I heard them stop. There is a sound a room makes when it stops waiting. It is the sound of a hundred people breathing together with nothing to breathe toward.

That my hands did not shake. Not once. I know because I noticed — from the edge, on the way out — that they were still, and that it was the only time tonight they had been still without the keys to steady them, because they were on the keys, and the keys were the railing, and I was walking along it over the water in the dark with my eyes shut and I did not fall.

That the pleasure was there. A bar early. Alone. Unholdable. The same as it has always been, the same as it was at eleven in a school hall and at twenty in a city I had just arrived in and at forty-eight in a rented room with sixty-one strangers. It did not know I was ill. It did not know I was old. It came a half-bar before every arrival and it was gone before the room caught up and it was — I will say this plainly — it was the same. Exactly the same. The one thing in me the water had not reached.

That across the room, on the eleventh platform, in the dark, a small boy sat with his feet over the water and listened, and that near the end — I felt this rather than saw it; there was nothing to see by — he stood up.
That is all I have.

I came up on a low note. The hands had gone down the soft way, further than they came, and settled, and stopped, and the violin let her line fall after mine and the cello let the floor down and the saxophone breathed out one last time and stopped, and there was the water, moving, and a hundred people not breathing, and dark.
I lifted my hands. Held them in the air a moment, the way you do. Put them in my lap. They began to shake, and I let them.
I did not know where I was.

I want that understood. I came up and the man came back into the room and he did not know the room. A piano. Dark. Water, somewhere. Three young people behind me with instruments, breathing. A hundred shapes on low platforms. A chair beside me with a woman in it — dark hair, a line between her brows — looking at me with a face that was doing something I had no word for.
I did not know her. I knew that I did not know her. I knew that I should.

I knew one other thing, and it was the only thing, and it was enough: that whatever I had just done, it had been good. Not good like a review. Good like warmth. The weather of it was still in me, whole, and the thing that had made it was gone entirely, and I sat in the dark with my hands shaking in my lap and the weather in my chest and thought, as clearly as I had thought anything all night:
Something’s happened, I think.
The woman stood up.
23. THE FRIENDS

They would try, afterwards, separately and together, to describe the last part of the night, and would fail, and would eventually stop trying and simply say to people: the lights went out. Which was not what happened. The lights were never on. That was the point, and it was the thing nobody who had not been there could be made to understand.

For the first eighty minutes the room had answered. Every short phrase the old man played had brought up its handful of lights across the dark water and let them go, and by the middle of the night the marsh had been a town, and then — around the time the woman in the chair had got up and gone out and come back, which neither of them understood and both of them had watched — the old man had stopped, and sat with his hands in his lap, and the lights had gone down, all of them, and had not come back.
And then he had played for ten minutes with nothing answering.
Her husband said, in the car, that it was like watching someone talk to a person who had died. She said no. It was like watching someone who had stopped needing to be answered.
The music was the most beautiful thing either of them had ever heard, and they could not have hummed you a bar of it.

Then it stopped. The old man lifted his hands and held them in the air and put them down, and the three young players let their sounds go one at a time, and the water moved, and nobody on any of the eleven platforms breathed, and the old man sat very still at the dark piano and looked — she saw this by the one small green light at the stage edge — looked round the room as if he had never seen it, and then at the woman beside him as if he had never seen her either.
And the woman in the chair stood up, and in the green light they saw her face for the first time.
“That’s her,” she said, into her husband’s ear. It was. Laleh.

She crossed the three steps to the piano. She did not hurry. She put her hand on the old man’s shoulder — her left hand, flat, as you put a hand on a wall to find it in the dark — and left it there. And she looked out at the room for the first time all night, at a hundred people she could not see, and she began to hum.

It was the four notes. The stairs. The thing the saxophone had turned into a woman’s voice in the middle of the night; the thing the old man had played twice, somewhere in the last hour, with no light answering. Laleh hummed it with her mouth shut and her hand on his shoulder, and it went up, and turned, and came down the soft way, further than it rose, and settled.
Then she sang it. With words.
And the room, which had been dark for ten minutes, began — very slowly — to answer her.

It was not the box. The box did not know this song and never would; they learned afterwards, in the tea room, that for those six minutes the lights had been run by hand, from a board at the back, by the people who had built the room and had rehearsed this with her in the empty afternoons.

Not the way it had answered him. They understood that much, even then. His lights had come in handfuls, scattered, sudden, and gone. Hers came one at a time, far off, as if from the back of a very long life. On the first verse — a courtyard holding its breath, a moon kept in water the way a mother keeps a child — a single bulb came up at the far end of the room, and held, and another, a long way from it, and that was all. The quiet years. The early ones, when nothing much is laid down and what is laid down is small.
Sleep. I am coming. I am coming at the end of the song.

Her voice was low and scratched and plain, not a singer’s voice, a voice that had been talking to someone for a year and was tired, and there was a sadness in it from the first line that did not ask for anything. The violin found her on the second verse and walked beside her. The cello laid the floor. The saxophone, far back, hummed, like a woman in a kitchen two rooms away. And the lights came a little faster — a few near the middle now, a few near the stage, their twins trembling in the water under them — the way memories come faster once a life has started to have things in it.
The piano is loud, and a mother at her music will not hear you fall.
Her husband’s hand found hers in the dark on that line. Neither of them knew yet why.

On the third verse she went almost to speaking, and the room held its lights where they were and added none — the line that I loved was so beautiful that I played it once more — and then, on the fourth, the piano under her began to climb, a slow figure going up the stairs and up them again in layers, and the lights began to come everywhere, dozens, hundreds, the marsh becoming the town they had watched it become an hour before, except that now they knew what they were watching: a life filling up. I have put down the keys. I will hum, and I will not play. By the end of the fourth verse the whole room was lit, two thousand small gold lights standing in the water and two thousand more under it, and the water itself was gold, and every face on every couch was turned up toward a woman with her hand on an old man’s shoulder.
Then the piano stopped climbing. A long pause. Rain, somewhere, on a roof — a hundred people breathing, not rain.
And she sang the last verse the way you would not have thought that voice could — up out of the chest, louder than anywhere before, breaking on the second word and going on anyway:
Laa-laa — no. Wake now. Wake now. Call to me through the wall.
There is no song. I am not at the keys. I am here. I hear it all.
And on the third line — Come to the door, little one — I have thrown it open wide — the lights began to go.

Not all at once. From the far end first, the way they had come, a slow wave of dark rolling toward the stage, street by street, the town going out behind her as she sang, until on the last line — There is nothing I am finishing. There is no one else inside. — there was one bulb left, low, near the piano, and she held the low note at the end until that one went too.
Dark. The quiet years again. The ones at the other end.
Nobody moved. Nobody breathed. She took her hand off his shoulder.
Then she spoke.

Someone had set a microphone on a stand beside the piano, and she took it from the stand and held it the way people hold a thing they do not often hold, and the green light showed her face, and she waited until she could.

“Thank you for coming,” she said. “I want to thank some people before I say anything else, because they’ll be gone tomorrow and I won’t get another chance in front of you. The people who built this — who flooded a floor and wired two thousand lights and stood every one of them in the water by hand, and who have taken you across that walkway ten at a time, three hundred nights, without losing anybody — and who ran the lights for me just now.” A sound from the room that was nearly a laugh. “The three people behind me. A violin that has learned to follow a man who doesn’t always know where he’s going. A cello that has been the floor of this room every night so the rest of us had something to stand on. And a saxophone that waits fifty minutes, every night, until the room starts talking, and then plays like a woman humming with her mouth shut.” She turned. “And the pianist.”
She stopped. The water.
“Who is my father.”
Nobody on the platforms made a sound. She let it sit.
“I’m going to tell you where the song came from, and then where the room came from, and then I’ll let you go.

“My grandmother was a pianist. In another country, a long time ago, she lost a child — her first — while she was playing, with a door pulled to so the music wouldn’t wake him. She never played again. She hummed instead, for fifty years, the same few notes, and never once got to the end of them, because the end was where it had happened. She wrote the words you just heard afterwards, for the child, and sang them once that anyone knows of, at the very end of her life, when she’d forgotten everything else. My father was in the room. He didn’t remember it. I did. I was seventeen.
“Then my father started humming.

“He never had. He was a man who played or was silent. And one morning he was at my kitchen counter with an orange in his hand, humming his mother’s four notes and stopping where she stopped, and he asked me what the thing in his hand was called. I put a phone on the counter that day. I’ve recorded him for six years. Thousands of pieces, a few seconds each. Every light that answered him tonight was one of them.

“He has a disease that comes and goes. Some nights he knows me. Most nights I’m his mother, and I let him think so, because she’s who he needs in the chair. It’s faster than hers was. There aren’t many lights left in him, and they’re far apart now — the way they are at the start of the night, one at the back, then one a long way from it. I built this while there were still some. I wanted him to have somewhere to go, every night, where it didn’t matter that they were going. And I wanted a hundred strangers a night to sit in what he feels — something that mattered, and no memory under it — because I couldn’t think of another way to show anyone where he lives.
“Tomorrow the water goes down the drain. He won’t remember this room. He doesn’t remember it now; he’s sitting there wondering who I am.
“But he’ll feel it. That’s the whole of what I’ve learned in a year. The feeling stays after the thing is gone. He’ll go home tonight warm, and not know why, and that’s what this was for.

“One more thing. Beside each of your platforms there’s a bulb that hasn’t been lit all night. It’s going to come on now. It’s yours. It’s the only light in this room that was made tonight instead of remembered, and it’s the one you get to take out with you. Thank you.”
She put the microphone back on the stand.

For a moment nothing happened. Then, from somewhere in the dark to their left, the sound of a person standing up off a couch. Then another. Then everywhere — a hundred people getting to their feet on wooden platforms over black water, in a dark so complete they could not see the person beside them, and the sound that came up out of it was not loud, it was not the sound of a concert hall, it was the sound of a hundred people who had been told something true and did not know what to do with their hands, and it went on for a long time, and she stood in the green light with her hands at her sides and let it.
And then, beside each platform, the large bulb on its stem came on.

Eleven warm lights, low over the water, one for each couch, doubled under themselves. Nothing on the stage. Nothing in the marsh. Only the lights that belonged to the audience now, warming the wood under their bare feet, showing each group of ten the faces of the strangers they had lain beside for ninety minutes and never seen, and showing them the walkway home.
Laleh went back to the piano.
She bent and said something to the old man. The two of them, on the nearest platform, with their own light warm beside them, were close enough to hear what he said back.
“Did we have a nice time?” the old man said. Pleasantly. The way you would ask a kind stranger about her evening.
“Yes,” she said. “We did.”

He nodded, and looked round at the eleven low lights and the dark between them and the woman in front of him, with the mild open interest of a man to whom everything has just arrived and who has not been told what any of it is for.
“I thought so,” he said. “I can feel it.”

She put her hand on his shoulder. Behind them the cello began, very low, the four notes, and the saxophone found them and hummed them back, with the reed barely touching, and no bulb on the stage answered either of them, and none would again.

He stood. He was taller than he had looked at the piano, and older, and he moved the way old men move who have been told to be careful of their feet, and she kept her hand on his shoulder and steered him, and the two of them went along the walkway away from the stage into a dark that had nothing in it, no lamp, no light, the hum of the cello and the saxophone going on behind them over the water until it was only the saxophone, and then only the water.
The two of them on the nearest platform watched until there was nothing to watch.
In the car her husband did not start the engine for a long time.

Thousands of lights. She knew that. She had watched them come and go for an hour and a half and she could not, sitting there with the heater on, remember a single one. Not one bulb. Not where it had been or when or what tune had lit it. They were gone the way the hours of your own life go: every one of them, and no funeral.
What she had instead was something she kept putting her hand to, flat, over the breastbone, the way you touch a pocket to check a thing is still there.
“What was that,” he said, eventually. Not a question.
“I don’t know.”
“Why did she keep her hand on his shoulder? The whole time. Even going out.”

She thought about it. She thought about a glass being looked into, a year ago, in a kitchen; about for someone; about a woman on a plain chair who had not, for as long as they could see her, taken her eyes off the back of an old man’s head.
“I think she was holding on,” she said.

He started the car. The street off the river was dark and the warehouse behind them was dark and the river itself, when they crossed it, was a flat black nothing with the city’s lights lying on it upside down.

It was a mile before either of them noticed they were both humming — four notes going up like stairs, and a turn at the top — and that neither of them had the faintest idea where they had learned it, and that neither of them stopped where the old man had always stopped. They went on down the soft way, further than it rose, and settled.

GLOSSARY

Alzheimer’s disease [ALTS-high-merz] — The most common of the diseases that take memory in old age. It damages the brain from the newest layers down, so that recent memories go first and the oldest — including music learned in childhood — go last.
Named for the German doctor who first described it.
Filament [FIL-a-ment] — The thin thread of wire inside an old-fashioned light bulb that glows when electricity passes through it.
Impostor feeling — Doctors call it Capgras syndrome [KAP-grah]: the conviction, in certain brain illnesses, that a loved one has been replaced by a stranger who looks the same. Named for the
French doctor who described it. The person feels it sincerely and is not being cruel.
Lewy body dementia [LOO-ee] — The second most common of the diseases that take the mind in old age. Caused by clumps of a protein inside brain cells, the same protein found in Parkinson’s.

It comes and goes from hour to hour, causes detailed silent visions of people and animals, stiffens and shakes the body, and is faster than Alzheimer’s. Named for the doctor who first saw the clumps under a microscope. Often misdiagnosed.

Lullaby — A song sung to a child to make it sleep. In Persian the word is lalaee [laa-laa-EE], and the traditional songs are often sadder than the child can understand; mothers have always sung their own griefs into them.
Maman [maa-MAAN] — Persian for Mother, as a child says it. The one word of his first language the pianist never gave up.
Tarpaulin [tar-PAW-lin] — A heavy waterproof canvas sheet for covering things outdoors.
Zone, the — What musicians call the state a skilled person enters when deep in a task: the self-watching part of the mind goes quiet, time goes wrong, and little is remembered afterwards.
